New dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance or arrhythmia may reflect rejection or graft failure. [2–4]
- **Remember silent ischaemia.** Cardiac denervation blunts angina; CAV can cause silent myocardial ischaemia/infarction, arrhythmia or graft dysfunction. Risk assessment should use clinical status and transplant follow-up, not absence of chest pain. [2–4]
- **Review immunosuppressants and organs.** Maintain tacrolimus/ciclosporin, mycophenolate and corticosteroids unless the transplant team directs otherwise; plan alternatives if nil-by-mouth. Check blood count, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, drug interactions/levels and infection or wound-healing risk. Coordinate major surgery with the transplant service. [3,4]

### Intraoperative

- **Denervated physiology.** Resting HR is often approximately 90–110/min. No rapid vagal or sympathetic reflex change in HR with hypovolaemia, pain, laryngoscopy or hypotension; some late reinnervation is possible. Output relies more heavily on venous return and circulating catecholamines. Do not use HR alone as a gauge of volume status or anaesthetic depth. [2,3]
- **Maintain haemodynamics.** Avoid abrupt reductions in preload/SVR (rapid induction, high neuraxial block, haemorrhage), but do not reflexively volume-load a failing graft. Choose GA or regional according to procedure and anticoagulation; add invasive monitoring for major surgery or impaired graft function. [2–4]
- **Choose effective rescue drugs.** Use direct-acting agents (noradrenaline, phenylephrine or adrenaline as appropriate) for hypotension; ephedrine may be less reliable. Atropine/glycopyrrolate may not raise HR; for significant bradycardia, prepare isoprenaline/adrenaline and pacing. ISHLT notes that sugammadex is a reasonable neuromuscular reversal option when appropriate. [3]
- **Asepsis and drug interactions.** Strict infection prevention; ensure appropriate antibiotics. Avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins and check interactions with calcineurin inhibitors (notably macrolides/azoles); immunosuppression can complicate healing and infection detection. [2–4]

### Postoperative

- **Protect graft and organs.** Restart scheduled immunosuppression promptly, verify drug dosing/troughs as indicated, and monitor renal function, electrolytes, glucose, fluid balance and infection/wound healing. Steroid supplementation, if required, depends on chronic exposure and adrenal suppression—not transplant status alone. [3,4]
- **Investigate deterioration early.** Hypotension, arrhythmia, reduced output or pulmonary oedema requires assessment for bleeding/sepsis, rejection, CAV-related ischaemia and graft dysfunction, with ECG, troponin/echo and transplant-team input as indicated. [2–4]

> **Key point:** a transplanted heart can have a normal EF yet no normal autonomic reflexes; think direct-acting vasoactives, careful loading, silent CAV, infection and uninterrupted immunosuppression.

## Selected linked references

- [1. Edwards S, Allen S, Sidebotham D. Anaesthesia for heart transplantation. BJA Education 2021;21:284–291.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.02.006)
- [2. Choudhury M. Post-cardiac transplant recipient: implications for anaesthesia. Indian J Anaesth 2017;61:768–774.](https://doi.org/10.4103/ija.IJA_390_17)
- [3. ISHLT. Guidelines for the care of heart transplant recipients. J Heart Lung Transplant 2023;42: e1–e141 (intercurrent surgery / Table 14).](https://www.ishlt.org/docs/default-source/standards-guidelines/2022_guideline_ishlt_careofhtxrecipients.pdf)
- [4. AHA/ACC et al. Guideline for perioperative cardiovascular management for noncardiac surgery. Circulation 2024 (Section 6.3.5).](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285)

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
These are not merely names to memorise. For each, know **who was studied, what intervention was compared, what the primary outcome showed, and what you must not over-extrapolate**. Trials from a non-cardiac surgery population or from acute MI shock do not automatically determine postcardiotomy practice.

| Trial | Topic | Key message |
|---|---|---|
| [CORONARY](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1601564) (Lamy et al., NEJM 2016, five-year follow-up) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 4,752 patients randomised to off- versus on-pump CABG. The five-year composite of death, stroke, MI, renal failure or repeat revascularisation was **23.1% versus 23.6%** (no significant difference). Use: operator experience, completeness of grafting and patient anatomy are important; off-pump is not uniformly safer. |
| [ROOBY five-year follow-up](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1614341) (Shroyer et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | In a largely male veteran population, five-year death was **15.2% off pump versus 11.9% on pump**. Use: apparently less invasive strategies can produce inferior long-term outcomes in certain contexts; do not generalise one trial to every centre. |
| [GOPCABE](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1211666) (Diegeler et al., NEJM 2013) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Elderly patients (≥75 years) having CABG: no major difference in primary composite outcomes at 30 days, although repeat revascularisation differed. Use: the operative method is not chosen on age alone. |
| [ATACAS tranexamic acid](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27774838/) (Myles et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | TXA in coronary surgery reduced blood product use (4,331 vs 7,994 units total) and reoperation for major haemorrhage/tamponade (1.4% vs 2.8%) **but increased seizures** (0.7% vs 0.1%). No statistically significant improvement in its primary composite thrombotic/death outcome. Use: give TXA for blood conservation with a sensible, renal-adjusted dose; seizures are dose/context related. |
| [TRICS III](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818) (Mazer et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 4,860 moderate/high-risk cardiac surgical patients; restrictive RBC transfusion trigger **Hb 7.5 g/dL** was non-inferior to liberal transfusion for death, MI, stroke and new dialysis (11.4% vs 12.5%). Use: restrictive transfusion is reasonable in stable patients; reassess active haemorrhage and ischaemia individually. |
| [TRICS III six-month follow-up](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30146969/) (Mazer et al., NEJM 2018) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Noninferiority of restrictive strategy persisted for the composite clinical outcome at six months. Use: reinforces that using less blood did not worsen the trial’s specified outcomes. |
| [TITRe2](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1403612) (Murphy et al., NEJM 2015) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Postoperative cardiac surgical patients allocated to different restrictive/liberal transfusion thresholds: no significant difference in the primary serious infection/ischaemic composite, but a mortality signal favoured the liberal group, creating earlier uncertainty. Use: contextualise subsequent TRICS III rather than pretending all cardiac transfusion evidence is identical. |
| [BART](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0802395) (Fergusson et al., NEJM 2008) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Compared antifibrinolytic agents in high-risk cardiac surgery; aprotinin associated with concerning mortality compared with lysine analogues. Use: the choice of antifibrinolytic is a safety decision; policy/regulatory status varies by jurisdiction. |
| [SIRS trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26460660/) (Whitlock et al., Lancet 2015) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 7,507 patients on CPB randomised to methylprednisolone versus placebo: no reduction in 30-day mortality or major morbidity. Use: routine prophylactic high-dose corticosteroid is not an evidence-based default for CPB-related inflammatory response. |
| [DECS](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14144) (Dieleman et al., JAMA 2012) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | High-dose dexamethasone in cardiac surgery did not significantly improve its composite major-adverse-event primary outcome, despite some secondary differences. Use: avoid translating anti-inflammatory biomarker changes into assured clinical benefit. |
| [TRACS](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.1446) (Hajjar et al., JAMA 2010) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Compared restrictive versus liberal transfusion based on haematocrit after cardiac surgery, finding no significant composite outcome difference in its sample. Use: original transfusion evidence is limited by selected patients, thresholds and statistical power. |
| [IABP-SHOCK II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24011548/) (Thiele et al., NEJM 2012; follow-up) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Around 600 patients with MI-related cardiogenic shock and planned early revascularisation: routine IABP did **not** lower 30-day or one-year mortality. Use: indications for IABP now focus on selected bridging physiology rather than a universal survival benefit. |
| [DanGer Shock](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572) (Møller et al., NEJM 2024) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Selected STEMI-related shock patients: Impella CP decreased 180-day mortality **45.8% vs 58.5%**, but increased severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis and renal replacement. Use: selected phenotype and procedure expertise are central; do not apply indiscriminately to postcardiotomy patients. |
| [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227) (Thiele et al., NEJM 2023) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Early VA-ECMO for infarct-related shock did not improve 30-day mortality (**47.8% vs 49.0%**); more bleeding and vascular complications. Use: ‘more flow’ does not guarantee improved survival and imposes a complication burden. |
| [ECMO-CS](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.122.062949) (Ošťádal et al., Circulation 2023) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Immediate VA-ECMO versus early conservative management with rescue ECMO in rapidly deteriorating severe cardiogenic shock; no clear improvement in the primary composite clinical outcome from immediate routine ECMO. Use: timely selected rescue rather than automatic cannulation. |
| [SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199908263410901) (Hochman et al., NEJM 1999) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Early coronary revascularisation in MI-associated cardiogenic shock improved longer-term outcomes even though the 30-day primary mortality difference was not statistically significant. Use: definitive correction of ischaemia remains fundamental; support devices are bridges. |
| [CESAR](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19762075/) (Peek et al., Lancet 2009) | VV-ECMO for respiratory failure | Randomised **referral to an ECMO-capable centre**, not ECMO itself in every patient: 63% versus 47% survived without severe disability at six months. Use: supports specialist service organisation/referral but does not isolate the benefit of the pump alone. |
| [EOLIA](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800385) (Combes et al., NEJM 2018) | VV-ECMO for respiratory failure | Severe ARDS: 60-day mortality **35% ECMO versus 46% control**, P=0.09 for prespecified primary comparison; 28% crossed over from control to rescue ECMO. Use: important signal underpowered/interpreted with crossover, not a definitive positive primary mortality trial. |
| [ERAS Cardiac Society consensus](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamasurg.2019.1153) (Engelman et al., JAMA Surgery 2019) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | Evidence-based expert recommendations for bundled cardiac enhanced recovery, including prehabilitation, opioid-sparing analgesia, glycaemic control and early mobilisation. Use: fast tracking is a pathway, not just extubation speed; this is consensus and mixed-level evidence rather than one mortality RCT. |
| [Temporary epicardial pacing](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003) (BJA Education 2023 clinical review) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | Not a landmark trial, but a high-yield illustrated teaching publication on pacing modes, threshold checks, capture/sensing and postoperative safety. Use: directly supports practical weaning and the 2026.1 examiner-style pacing question. |
| [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | High-impact evidence synthesis rather than a clinical trial: perfusion, temperature, neurological protection, circuit safety, anticoagulation and myocardial protection. Use: this is the best contemporary synthesis for the technical CPB sections. |

items.title: References by subtopic
items.body:
## BJA Education reading guide: what to read and why

- **1.** [Principles of cardiopulmonary bypass](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/6/5/176/337119) (BJA Education, 2006). **Start here for the circuit.** Older but exceptionally useful for how venous drainage, pump, oxygenator, heat exchange and cannulation actually work; update practice thresholds from the 2024 CPB guideline.
- **2.** [Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part one — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003) (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for heparin, ACT, resistance, rebound and protamine.** Read with the anticoagulation chapter and repeat the protamine-reaction differential aloud.
- **3.** [Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part two — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.03.008) (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for HIT and alternatives to heparin.** Particularly useful for distinguishing expected post-CPB thrombocytopenia from HIT and managing bivalirudin on bypass.
- **4.** [Temporary epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003) (BJA Education, 2023). **Essential for pacing, weaning and ICU capture troubleshooting**; directly relevant to recent ANZCA questions.
- **5.** [Anaesthesia for adult cardiac surgery requiring repeat sternotomy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.10.001) (BJA Education, 2024). **Best set-specific reading for SS_CS 1.15**: CT, previous grafts, emergency access, pre-sternotomy CPB and haemorrhage.
- **6.** [Perioperative care in cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.05.008) (BJA Education, 2021). **Best for fast-track/ERAS concepts**, sedation, analgesia, mobilisation and recovery care.
- **7.** [Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe acute respiratory failure](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001) (BJA Education, 2024). **Practical VV-ECMO overview**: referral, indications, oxygenation/sweep, ventilation and weaning.
- **8.** [Physiology of VV-ECMO, Part 1: terminology, circuits and gas exchange](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.003) (BJA Education, 2026). **Best newer physiology-focused follow-up**; useful for explaining recirculation, blood-flow versus sweep effects and oxygen delivery.
- **9.** [Management of cardiogenic shock after acute coronary syndromes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.01.006) (BJA Education, 2023). **Use for MCS physiology** and the distinction between revascularisation, pressors/inotropy and device-supported circulatory rescue; update device trial interpretation using DanGer Shock/ECLS-SHOCK.
- **10.** [Anaesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.06.004) (BJA Education, 2018). **Useful for procedure variations, cannulation, positioning and TOE**; supplement with contemporary techniques and local practice.
- **11.** [Pulmonary artery catheterisation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.08.003) (BJA Education, 2024). **Useful for haemodynamic phenotyping** of LV versus RV failure and the limits of filling pressures; read selectively alongside the difficult-weaning chapter.
## ANZCA Blue Book, guidelines, examiner reports and reference texts

### ANZCA and Australasian sources

- [ANZCA — Anaesthesia training program curriculum, Appendix Five](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/all-handbooks-and-curriculums/anzca-anaesthesia-training-program-curriculum.pdf). Source of exact Final Examination learning outcomes; the workbook determines which components belong to Set 13.
- [ANZCA — PG27(A), Guideline for major extracorporeal perfusion](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents). Australasian professional framework for safe major extracorporeal perfusion. Local team protocols should operationalise the details.
- [ANZCA — PG46, perioperative echocardiography (2025)](https://libguides.anzca.edu.au/anaestrain/ssu/cardiac). Practice and competency standards for echocardiography use; relevant to diagnosis during difficult separation and ICU instability.
- [Hegde S, Pearse B, Santifort K et al. Goal-directed bleeding management: understanding and implementing viscoelastic haemostatic assays across patient blood management](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387). Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025, pages 59 onwards. Core source for applying ROTEM/TEG to actively bleeding patients and avoiding indiscriminate product administration.
- [Johnstone L. The perioperative management of lung transplantation](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/bitstream/11055/1305/5/00_2025_Blue_Book.pdf). Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025. Relevant application of VA-ECMO/CPB versus off-pump support in non-cardiac/thoracic surgery; use as a clinical example, not as a universal transplant protocol.
- [CALS-ANZ: Australasian ANZSCTS/ANZICS cardiothoracic advanced life support](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10692601/). Source for cardiac surgical postoperative arrest management, pacing/shocks and the importance of trained early resternotomy.
- **ANZCA Final Examination chair reports:** 2019.2 Question 1 on DHCA (rationale and physiology); 2016.2 and 2012.2 questions on separation from CPB; 2026.1 Question 7 on epicardial pacing and loss of capture. The reports complement current guidelines but are **exam-expectation sources**, not practice guidelines.
### Current specialty guidelines

- [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on cardiopulmonary bypass in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354) (published 2025). Primary modern reference for circuit, perfusion flow, temperature, cerebral/myocardial protection and CPB safety.
- [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on patient blood management](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae352) (published 2025). Primary reference for transfusion, antifibrinolytics, haemostasis, protamine, VHA and postoperative bleeding.
- [2024 EACTS Guidelines on perioperative medication in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae355). Relevant to preoperative antithrombotic decisions and postoperative resumption of therapy.
- [ELSO guidelines and resources](https://www.elso.org/ecmo-resources/elso-ecmo-guidelines.aspx), including the 2021 adult VV respiratory failure guidance. Relevant to ECMO referral, patient selection, circuit and weaning; centres should use their latest approved protocols.
- [2025 ERC Guidelines — special circumstances in resuscitation](https://www.resus.org.uk/professional-library/2025-resuscitation-guidelines/special-circumstances-guidelines). Relevant to arrest in patients early after cardiac surgery, rapid shocks/pacing and expert resternotomy.
- [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/). For current valve-treatment decisions and prosthesis context; the actual cardiac-surgery anaesthetic sequence is explained in Chapters 2–3.
- [Australasian VV-ECMO clinical practice guideline (2026)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12955552/). Australia/New Zealand GRADE guidance on selecting adults with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure; conditional recommendation and explicit assessment of longer-term neurological and functional outcomes.
- [2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for valvular heart disease](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/44/4635/8234488). Prosthetic valve selection and postoperative anticoagulation; useful with the surgical-procedure chapters.
### Authoritative textbooks for deeper reading

The guidance and articles above were directly searchable; the following are **recommended authoritative textbooks**, not claims that their entire chapters were available for direct line-by-line verification here:
- Kaplan’s Cardiac Anesthesia — cardiopulmonary bypass, myocardial protection, difficult separation, cardiac surgical haemodynamics and TOE.
- Miller’s Anesthesia — cardiac anaesthesia and extracorporeal circulation sections, ventilation and postoperative critical care.
- Cardiopulmonary Bypass: Principles and Practice (Gravlee et al.) — fundamental perfusion science, pump/oxygenator physiology and myocardial protection.
- Clinical Perfusion for Cardiac Surgery: A Step-by-Step Guide to the Fundamentals (Awad, DiNardo, Huang, Hancock; 2026) — particularly useful for the perfusionist’s perspective and circuit troubleshooting.

**Set 13 curriculum coverage check:** SS_CS 1.1 (Chapter 6); 1.3 (Chapter 2); 1.5 and 1.7 (Chapters 2–3); 1.9 (Chapter 7); 1.15 (Chapter 2); 1.16 (Chapter 9); 1.17 (Chapters 1, 4–7); 1.18 (Chapter 5); 1.19 (Chapter 7); 1.20, 1.21, 1.22 and 1.23 (Chapters 10–11); 1.27 (Chapter 12); 1.28 (Chapter 8); SS_IC 1.39 (Chapter 8); SS_IC 1.62 (Chapter 9). All 18 workbook outcome rows are represented without importing unrelated Set 14 vascular surgery material.

## Evidence and source key (Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content)

- **bb25**: [Blue Book 2025: Goal-directed bleeding management, pp59–79](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_Blue_Book_PDF.pdf?language=en)

items.title: List the prerequisites for separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: List the prerequisites for separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.
items.a:
- Rate and rhythm stable (sinus or paced, 80 to 100); contractility and volume adequate; MAP above 65.
- Lungs re-expanded and ventilating with FiO2 1.0.
- Temperature above 36 °C; acid-base, K, calcium and Hb corrected; coagulation addressed.
- Adequate anaesthesia; pacing wires, defibrillator and drugs ready.

> **Closing point:** Heart, lungs, metabolic state, equipment.

items.title: What are the causes of hypotension immediately after separation from bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What are the causes of hypotension immediately after separation from bypass?
items.a:
- Pump failure: LV stunning or ischaemia, RV failure, valve problem.
- Rate and rhythm disturbance, heart block.
- Preload: hypovolaemia, bleeding, tamponade, tension pneumothorax.
- Afterload: vasoplegia, protamine reaction, anaphylaxis.

> **Closing point:** Use TOE to tell them apart.

items.title: What are the first steps when a patient fails to wean from bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What are the first steps when a patient fails to wean from bypass?
items.a:
- Maintain/restore adequate CPB flow and systemic perfusion; vent to prevent ventricular distension.
- Check rhythm/pacing, temperature, blood gases, electrolytes, ventilation and anaesthesia.
- TOE/direct inspection: LV/RV, valves/LVOTO, filling, air, tamponade; check grafts and surgical causes.
- Treat the cause and reassess before another wean; select IABP for appropriate LV problems, RVAD or VA-ECMO for severe RV/biventricular failure.

> **Closing point:** Diagnose the mechanism while maintaining perfusion.

items.title: How do you recognise and treat right ventricular failure after bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: How do you recognise and treat right ventricular failure after bypass?
items.a:
- Low output with a dilated poorly contracting RV, septal shift and often high CVP/TR; PA pressure may be high or fall in advanced failure.
- Consider pre-existing PH, RV ischaemia/coronary air, poor protection, valve dysfunction; protamine only if given.
- Optimise filling/AV synchrony, oxygenation, CO2 and pH; support pressure with noradrenaline/vasopressin and contractility with a titrated inotrope.
- Inhaled NO/prostacyclin for high PVR; restore CPB and consider RVAD/VA-ECMO early if refractory. IABP gives no direct RV flow.

> **Closing point:** Avoid both RV overfilling and loss of coronary perfusion.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2021

items.title: What is vasoplegia after bypass and how is it treated?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What is vasoplegia after bypass and how is it treated?
items.a:
- Vasopressor-dependent hypotension with low SVR and preserved/high output after CPB; exclude bleeding, tamponade, pump failure, anaphylaxis and drug effects.
- Inflammation/NO signalling, relative vasopressin deficiency and catecholamine hyporesponsiveness contribute.
- Optimise filling; titrate noradrenaline and add low-dose vasopressin early when appropriate.
- Refractory cases: specialist methylene blue (check serotonergic drugs/G6PD deficiency/PH), hydroxocobalamin or angiotensin II. Steroids are selected adjuncts, not routine proven therapy for isolated post-CPB vasoplegia.

> **Closing point:** Follow organ perfusion as well as MAP.

> **Source:** CPB guideline 2024/2025

items.title: How do you set up epicardial pacing for complete heart block?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: How do you set up epicardial pacing for complete heart block?
items.a:
- DDD if sinus atrial activity and reliable atrial/ventricular wires; VVI if AF. Explain AV synchrony and haemodynamic benefit.
- Start an individual rate, often around 80–100/min, and optimise AV delay/output to perfusion and filling.
- Set output with a margin, commonly 2–3 times a safely assessed capture threshold; **lower sensing mV = more sensitive**.
- Confirm mechanical capture. Dependent patients need backup pacing before risky threshold testing. Asynchronous mode is monitored rescue/EMI management, with competitive-pacing risk.

> **Closing point:** Justify mode/rate and protect the dependent patient.

> **Source:** Exam report 2026.1

items.title: How do you troubleshoot intermittent failure to capture in a pacing-dependent patient?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: How do you troubleshoot intermittent failure to capture in a pacing-dependent patient?
items.a:
- Safety first: assess perfusion, call help, increase output and establish backup pacing; do not deliberately lose capture in a dependent patient.
- Patient: hypoxia, K/Mg, acidosis, temperature, ischaemia and threshold-raising drugs.
- Lead/generator: connections, polarity, dedicated return if unipolar, cable, battery, output and mode.
- Spikes without QRS = noncapture; absent inappropriate spikes may be oversensing. Adjust sensing (higher mV for oversensing); monitored asynchronous pacing can bypass inhibition.
- Transcutaneous bridge, urgent transvenous/new epicardial wires and EP review. Chronotropes bridge; atropine often fails in infranodal block.

> **Closing point:** Patient, lead, generator—with backup from the outset.

> **Source:** Exam report 2026.1

items.title: What are the effects of protamine on the right ventricle?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What are the effects of protamine on the right ventricle?
items.a:
- Protamine can cause acute pulmonary vasoconstriction/PH and RV failure, as well as vasodilatory hypotension or anaphylaxis.
- Stop administration, call help, support oxygenation/systemic perfusion and RV contractility; use inhaled pulmonary vasodilator when indicated.
- If refractory, re-heparinise and return to CPB with the team; treat anaphylaxis when present.
- Give reversal slowly **after successful separation**, titrated to residual heparin; slow dosing reduces some reactions but does not abolish risk.

> **Closing point:** Diagnose the reaction rather than giving more protamine automatically.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2023

items.title: What TOE findings would you look for when weaning from bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What TOE findings would you look for when weaning from bypass?
items.a:
- LV function and regional wall motion, filling and outflow obstruction.
- RV size/function using multiple measures (TAPSE alone is limited after cardiac surgery), septal position, tricuspid regurgitation.
- Valve function and paravalvular leak; air in the chambers.
- Pericardial collection and aortic integrity.

> **Closing point:** TOE is the main tool for the difficult wean.

items.title: How does an intra-aortic balloon pump work?
items.q: How does an intra-aortic balloon pump work?
items.a:
- Balloon in the descending aorta inflates in diastole and deflates before systole.
- Augments diastolic pressure and coronary flow; lowers afterload and oxygen demand.
- Provides modest variable assistance; needs native ejection. AF/pacing may need adapted triggering, not automatic exclusion.
- Triggered by ECG or arterial waveform.

> **Closing point:** Diastolic augmentation and systolic unloading.

items.title: List the indications for an IABP.
items.q: List the indications for an IABP.
items.a:
- Selected LV failure/shock as a bridge; **not routine for uncomplicated AMI shock** (IABP-SHOCK II).
- Failure to wean from bypass; post-infarction.
- Mechanical complications: acute MR, VSD.
- High-risk revascularisation; LV decompression on VA-ECMO.

> **Closing point:** A bridge to recovery or definitive treatment.

> **Source:** Exam report 2008.2

items.title: List the contraindications to an IABP.
items.q: List the contraindications to an IABP.
items.a:
- More than mild aortic regurgitation.
- Aortic dissection; significant aneurysmal/other aortic disease needs expert anatomical assessment.
- Severe aorto-iliac or peripheral vascular disease.
- Relative: coagulopathy, local sepsis.

> **Closing point:** Even mild regurgitation can worsen.

> **Source:** Exam report 2008.2

items.title: How is IABP timing set and what are the errors?
items.q: How is IABP timing set and what are the errors?
items.a:
- Inflate at the dicrotic notch; deflate just before systole.
- Early inflation closes the aortic valve early; late inflation reduces augmentation.
- Early deflation loses unloading; late deflation increases afterload.
- Correct position distal to the left subclavian artery; choose a reliable trigger and adapt it for AF/pacing.

> **Closing point:** Check the waveform on a 1:2 ratio.

items.title: What are the complications of an IABP?
items.q: What are the complications of an IABP?
items.a:
- Limb ischaemia (commonest), bleeding and retroperitoneal haematoma.
- Thrombocytopenia and haemolysis.
- Aortic dissection, stroke or embolism, visceral or left arm malperfusion.
- Infection and balloon rupture.

> **Closing point:** Check limb perfusion every hour.

items.title: What types of durable LVAD exist and how do they work?
items.q: What types of durable LVAD exist and how do they work?
items.a:
- Current durable example: HeartMate 3, fully magnetically levitated centrifugal pump. HeartMate II is legacy axial; HVAD was withdrawn from new implants in 2021.
- Drain LV apex and return blood through an **outflow graft** to the aorta; the **driveline carries power/control**, not blood.
- Little or no pulse; preload and afterload dependent.
- Indications: bridge to transplant or candidacy, recovery, destination therapy.

> **Closing point:** Pulse and standard monitoring are unreliable.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the anaesthetic principles for a patient with an LVAD?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic principles for a patient with an LVAD?
items.a:
- **Preop:** VAD-team plan, review RV/device function, alarms, power and antithrombotics. Individualise warfarin interruption/bridging; HM3 does not automatically require aspirin after ARIES-HM3.
- **Intraop:** reliable BP/perfusion monitoring, protect RV/preload, avoid excessive afterload/PVR, and monitor controller/power. Use low insufflation pressure for laparoscopy.
- Low-flow alarms require cause assessment (volume, RV failure, tamponade, obstruction, rhythm); do not give fluid blindly.
- **Postop:** monitored recovery, check device/CIED therapies, resume indicated antithrombotics when haemostasis permits.

> **Closing point:** Major warfarin bleeding may require 4F-PCC plus IV vitamin K with urgent VAD input.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2021

items.title: What are the complications of an LVAD?
items.q: What are the complications of an LVAD?
items.a:
- Bleeding (gastrointestinal, intracranial) and infection of the driveline.
- Stroke, pump thrombosis.
- Right heart failure and arrhythmia.
- Aortic regurgitation and device malfunction.

> **Closing point:** Bleeding and infection dominate.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2021

items.title: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.q: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.a:
- IABP: modest counterpulsation assistance; requires native ejection and accurate timing.
- Impella: directly pumps LV to aorta/unloads LV; model-dependent flow; needs adequate RV filling and has haemolysis/bleeding/vascular risks.
- VA-ECMO: circulatory plus gas-exchange support; raises LV afterload and may need selective unloading.
- Trials differ: IABP-SHOCK II and routine early ECLS-SHOCK were neutral; **DanGer-Shock showed a survival benefit in selected STEMI shock**, with more complications.

> **Closing point:** Match physiology, evidence population and an exit strategy.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2023

items.title: What are the indications for VV ECMO?
items.q: What are the indications for VV ECMO?
items.a:
- Severe potentially reversible respiratory failure despite optimal lung-protective care and proning where appropriate.
- Consider ELSO thresholds: P/F <80 mmHg, or pH <7.25 with PaCO2 ≥60 despite safe ventilator optimisation; refer early.
- Selected asthma, graft failure, pulmonary haemorrhage or transplant bridge may qualify.
- EOLIA’s 60-day mortality difference (35% vs 46%, P=0.09) was not statistically significant; CESAR tested an ECMO-centre referral strategy.

> **Closing point:** P/F alone does not imply a fixed predicted mortality.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2017

items.title: Compare VV and VA ECMO.
items.q: Compare VV and VA ECMO.
items.a:
- VV: drains the vena cava, returns to the right atrium; respiratory support only.
- VA: drains venous blood, returns to an artery; supports circulation and oxygenation.
- VA risks: increased LV afterload, differential hypoxia, limb ischaemia.
- Anticoagulation is usual, but intensity/temporary interruption depends on bleeding, circuit and centre protocol.

> **Closing point:** Choose by whether the heart needs support.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2017

items.title: What are the complications of ECMO?
items.q: What are the complications of ECMO?
items.a:
- Bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage.
- Circuit clotting, haemolysis, air embolism.
- Limb ischaemia (VA), infection, renal injury.
- Harlequin syndrome in peripheral VA ECMO.

> **Closing point:** Intracranial haemorrhage is the most devastating.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2017

items.title: Which non-cardiac surgeries may need bypass or ECMO support?
items.q: Which non-cardiac surgeries may need bypass or ECMO support?
items.a:
- Tumour with caval or atrial extension.
- Critical airway or tracheal surgery; lung transplant.
- Massive pulmonary embolism; rewarming after severe hypothermia.
- Cardiac arrest (E-CPR).

> **Closing point:** A plan for cannulation and anticoagulation is needed.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2017

items.title: What are the common causes of low cardiac output after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What are the common causes of low cardiac output after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Myocardial stunning or ischaemia from graft failure.
- Tamponade, hypovolaemia and bleeding.
- RV failure, arrhythmia and heart block.
- Tension pneumothorax and valve dysfunction; vasoplegia can coexist with low output, but isolated vasoplegia has preserved/high output.

> **Closing point:** TOE and a PA catheter help sort the cause.

items.title: How do you recognise and treat tamponade after cardiac surgery?
items.q: How do you recognise and treat tamponade after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Falling drain output, rising CVP, narrow pulse pressure, hypotension.
- Echo (TOE) shows localised clot; drains may be blocked.
- Emergency resternotomy; drainage.
- In arrest, resternotomy within 5 minutes.

> **Closing point:** Consider tamponade in any low output state.

items.title: How is bleeding managed after cardiac surgery?
items.q: How is bleeding managed after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Separate surgical bleeding and coagulopathy; they often coexist. Assess perfusion, drainage/patency and tamponade; call the surgeon early.
- Restore temperature, ionised calcium and pH; use labs/TEG/ROTEM to distinguish heparin effect from platelet, fibrinogen or factor deficits.
- Give targeted products and renal-adjusted TXA under the cardiac protocol; no universal “<100 mg/kg is safe” ceiling.
- Urgent re-exploration for tamponade/instability or ongoing surgical bleeding. FARES-II supports targeted 4F-PCC over plasma for post-CPB factor-deficient bleeding.

> **Closing point:** Product treatment must not delay surgical haemostasis.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2021

items.title: What is the incidence and treatment of AF after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What is the incidence and treatment of AF after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- About 30%, peaking on days 2 to 3.
- Correct K and Mg; beta-blocker or amiodarone.
- Synchronised cardioversion if unstable.
- Anticoagulation is individualised to AF duration/persistence, thromboembolic risk and early postoperative bleeding; arrange reassessment rather than automatic treatment by score alone.

> **Closing point:** Check electrolytes first.

items.title: What is the risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What is the risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Common and procedure/definition-dependent; severe dialysis-requiring AKI is less common.
- Mechanisms: hypoperfusion/hypoxia, venous congestion, ischaemia–reperfusion, haemolysis, inflammation and oxidative stress.
- CKD, diabetes, anaemia, poor ventricular function and complex/prolonged CPB increase risk.
- Use the KDIGO bundle and goal-directed CPB oxygen delivery; avoid hyperthermia/nephrotoxins and fluid overload. PROTECTION showed less creatinine-defined AKI with IV amino acids, without established mortality/dialysis benefit.

> **Closing point:** KDIGO includes a creatinine rise over **48 hours or 7 days**, or sustained oliguria.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2026

items.title: Which neurological complications follow cardiac surgery?
items.q: Which neurological complications follow cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Stroke (1 to 3%) and TIA; delirium and cognitive decline.
- Embolic, hypoperfusion and inflammatory mechanisms.
- Strategies: no-touch aorta, MAP targets, avoid hyperthermia, NIRS.
- Delirium screening and avoidance of benzodiazepines.

> **Closing point:** Aortic manipulation is a key embolic source.

items.title: Which factors influence the duration of ventilation after cardiac surgery?
items.q: Which factors influence the duration of ventilation after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Patient: age, COPD, obesity, poor LV function, renal disease.
- Surgical: emergency, redo, long CPB, bleeding.
- Anaesthetic: long-acting opioids, hypothermia, residual block.
- Postoperative: instability, lung injury, AKI, delirium.

> **Closing point:** Enhanced recovery is individualised; early extubation depends on present stability and readiness, not preoperative risk alone.

items.title: What is fast-track cardiac anaesthesia?
items.q: What is fast-track cardiac anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Early extubation within about 6 hours.
- Short-acting drugs and multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia.
- Normothermia, minimal bleeding, haemodynamic stability.
- Now part of enhanced recovery (ERAS Cardiac) with early mobilisation.

> **Closing point:** Do not extubate an unstable or bleeding patient to meet a target.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2021

items.title: What are the issues with redo cardiac surgery?
items.q: What are the issues with redo cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Re-entry risk: patent LIMA graft or RV behind the sternum.
- CT planning; prepare peripheral access/cannulation, with CPB before sternotomy in selected high-risk re-entry anatomy.
- External pads, large-bore access, blood and cell salvage ready.
- Longer CPB, more bleeding, higher mortality.

> **Closing point:** Prepare for haemorrhage at re-entry.

items.title: Outline the surgical steps of coronary artery bypass grafting.
items.q: Outline the surgical steps of coronary artery bypass grafting.
items.a:
- Sternotomy, conduit harvest (LIMA, radial, saphenous vein).
- Heparin, cannulation, bypass, cross-clamp and cardioplegia.
- Distal and proximal anastomoses, rewarming and weaning.
- Protamine, haemostasis, pacing wires and chest closure.

> **Closing point:** Off-pump avoids CPB; only a specifically anaortic technique avoids aortic manipulation/clamping.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic hazards of off-pump CABG, and when should the team convert to CPB?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic hazards of off-pump CABG, and when should the team convert to CPB?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- The stabiliser immobilises a target while **heart elevation/rotation** can impair RV filling, venous return, LV ejection and provoke MR or regional ischaemia; lateral and inferior targets are often least tolerated.
- **First action in collapse:** tell the surgeon to release/reduce displacement, restore preload and coronary perfusion, check ST changes and TOE; use an intracoronary shunt if appropriate. Avoid indiscriminate large fluid boluses.
- Convert to CPB for **sustained low output, refractory ischaemia or arrhythmia, unsafe target exposure or incomplete revascularisation** despite corrective manoeuvres.
- Off-pump does **not** inherently mean anaortic: side-biting clamps for proximal graft anastomoses can still embolise plaque. A specifically **anaortic/no-touch** strategy avoids aortic instrumentation.

> **Closing point:** In off-pump hypotension, release mechanical displacement before simply increasing drugs.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What did CORONARY and ROOBY show about on-pump versus off-pump CABG?
items.q: What did CORONARY and ROOBY show about on-pump versus off-pump CABG?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **CORONARY (five-year follow-up):** in 4,752 randomised CABG patients, the composite of death, stroke, MI, renal failure or repeat revascularisation was **23.1% off-pump vs 23.6% on-pump**, without a significant difference.
- **ROOBY (five-year follow-up):** in a predominantly male veteran population, death was **15.2% off-pump vs 11.9% on-pump**, favouring on-pump in that setting.
- **Interpretation:** surgeon/centre experience, target anatomy, complete revascularisation and aortic manipulation matter. Off-pump is **not universally better**; trial findings should not be extrapolated uncritically to every centre.

> **Closing point:** Avoid claiming that eliminating CPB always reduces important long-term outcomes.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What are the haemodynamic goals for coronary artery bypass anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic goals for coronary artery bypass anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Maintain coronary perfusion pressure.
- Heart rate 60 to 80; avoid tachycardia.
- Avoid hypotension and hypertension; treat ischaemia.
- Continue indicated beta-blocker; individualise ACEI/ARB continuation/withholding and hypotension planning.

> **Closing point:** Balance oxygen supply and demand.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic goals in severe aortic stenosis?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic goals in severe aortic stenosis?
items.a:
- Maintain sinus rhythm and preload.
- Maintain afterload and coronary perfusion; use phenylephrine or noradrenaline.
- Avoid tachycardia and bradycardia.
- Synchronised cardioversion for unstable AF; individualise stable AF rate/rhythm and thromboembolic management.

> **Closing point:** A fixed obstruction needs a fixed pressure head.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic considerations for TAVI?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations for TAVI?
items.a:
- Hybrid theatre with surgical and perfusion back-up.
- Local with sedation or GA; TOE with GA.
- Ballooning/deployment may require rapid pacing, depending on valve/technique; confirm capture and anticipate hypotension with a rescue plan.
- Complications: vascular injury, annular rupture, conduction block, stroke, leak.

> **Closing point:** Plan for conversion to open surgery.

items.title: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and TAVI.
items.q: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and TAVI.
items.a:
- Surgical AVR: younger, low risk, bicuspid, concomitant surgery.
- 2025 ESC/EACTS: suitable tricuspid AS at age ≥70 generally favours TAVI; <70 and low surgical risk favours SAVR. Other cases require individual/lifetime planning; TAVI is not limited to high surgical risk.
- TAVI risks: pacemaker, vascular injury, leak, stroke.
- Heart Team decision using STS or EuroSCORE.

> **Closing point:** Selection is a team decision.

items.title: Outline the surgical steps of mitral repair versus replacement and their anaesthetic implications.
items.q: Outline the surgical steps of mitral repair versus replacement and their anaesthetic implications.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- Both usually involve **CPB, cross-clamp and cardioplegia**, followed by left atriotomy or transseptal entry and inspection of leaflets, annulus, chordae and papillary apparatus.
- **Repair** may involve an annuloplasty ring, leaflet resection or neochordae; **replacement** implants a prosthesis, preferably preserving chordae/subvalvular structures where feasible to maintain LV geometry.
- After reperfusion, TOE assesses **residual MR, transmitral gradient, leaflet/prosthesis motion, paravalvular leak, RV/LV function and SAM/LVOTO**. Significant residual lesions may need immediate revision.
- In **MS**, avoid tachycardia, high PVR and loss of atrial contribution; in chronic **MR**, EF can overestimate true forward LV function. After correcting MR, anticipate **afterload mismatch**, while repair adds the possibility of SAM.

> **Closing point:** Mitral repair changes both valve geometry and the LV's effective afterload.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: After mitral repair, how do you distinguish LV afterload mismatch from SAM-related LVOT obstruction?
items.q: After mitral repair, how do you distinguish LV afterload mismatch from SAM-related LVOT obstruction?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Afterload mismatch:** removing the low-impedance regurgitant LA outlet suddenly increases **effective LV afterload**; TOE shows impaired LV systolic performance with low forward output, despite an adequately corrected valve.
- **SAM/LVOTO:** TOE shows a **small, hyperdynamic LV**, anterior leaflet/chordal motion towards the septum, dynamic LVOT gradient and often **posteriorly directed MR**. It worsens with hypovolaemia, tachycardia, reduced SVR or beta-agonists.
- For **afterload mismatch**, assess filling/ischaemia and provide appropriately titrated LV support. For **SAM**, **reduce inotropy**, restore SVR with a vasoconstrictor, correct genuine underfilling and slow HR if tolerated; ask the surgeon to revise repair if persistent.

> **Closing point:** A vigorous LV with hypotension and new MR may need less adrenaline, not more.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What monitoring is used for a standard cardiac surgical case?
items.q: What monitoring is used for a standard cardiac surgical case?
items.a:
- ECG with ST analysis, arterial line before induction, CVC (± PAC).
- TOE, NIRS, temperature, urine output.
- ACT, blood gases, glucose and haemoglobin.
- Pacing wires and defibrillator pads.

> **Closing point:** Arterial monitoring is often established before induction; CVC/PAC/TOE timing and use depend on risk and procedure.

items.title: How would you reduce anxiety in a patient presenting for cardiac surgery?
items.q: How would you reduce anxiety in a patient presenting for cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Clear information and honest discussion of expectations.
- Pre-op education, prehabilitation, avoid routine sedative premedication.
- Anxiolysis only if needed, taking care to avoid hypoventilation.
- Plan for early mobilisation and pain control.

> **Closing point:** Clear information and an individual support plan; reserve sedative drugs for selected patients.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2021

items.title: What are the components of a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit?
items.q: What are the components of a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit?
items.a:
- Venous cannula and reservoir.
- Pump (roller or centrifugal).
- Membrane oxygenator with heat exchanger.
- Arterial filter and return cannula.

> **Closing point:** Blood leaves the right atrium and returns to the aorta.

items.title: Calculate indexed oxygen delivery on CPB and explain why a normal MAP can mislead.
items.q: Calculate indexed oxygen delivery on CPB and explain why a normal MAP can mislead.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Indexed DO₂ (mL/min/m²) = pump flow index (L/min/m²) × arterial O₂ content (mL/dL) × 10**.
- **CaO₂ ≈ 1.34 × Hb (g/dL) × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂ (mmHg)**. Hb-bound O₂ dominates.
- At **Hb 8 g/dL, SaO₂ 100%, pump flow index 2.4 L/min/m²**, CaO₂ ≈ 10.7 mL/dL and **indexed DO₂ ≈ 257 ≈ 260 mL/min/m²** (before the small dissolved fraction).
- Normothermic goal-directed perfusion protocols commonly target about **280–300 mL/min/m²**, but not as an absolute safe threshold. Assess Hb, flow, SvO₂, lactate, temperature, cerebral oximetry and organs together.
- **MAP largely reflects flow × SVR**; vasoconstriction can raise MAP without improving an inadequate flow/Hb-derived DO₂.

> **Closing point:** Deliver adequate oxygen, not merely an attractive arterial pressure.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: Compare alpha-stat and pH-stat blood-gas management during hypothermic CPB.
items.q: Compare alpha-stat and pH-stat blood-gas management during hypothermic CPB.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Consensus on hypothermia in aortic arch surgery (temperature definitions)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3741830/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Alpha-stat:** interpret and target blood-gas values as measured at **37°C** without temperature correction. During cooling, actual in-vivo PaCO₂ falls and pH rises; cerebral autoregulation and protein charge regulation tend to be preserved. Common in **adult CPB**.
- **pH-stat:** add CO₂ during cooling so **temperature-corrected** pH ≈ 7.40 and PaCO₂ ≈ 40 mmHg. Cerebral vasodilation can improve cooling uniformity but may increase embolic delivery and blunt autoregulation.
- pH-stat has a role in selected **paediatric/deep-cooling** protocols; neither is universally superior for every operation.

> **Closing point:** The difference is which temperature the blood gas is interpreted at—and how CO₂ changes cerebral flow.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: Name three life-threatening CPB circuit emergencies and the immediate response to each.
items.q: Name three life-threatening CPB circuit emergencies and the immediate response to each.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Falling venous reservoir / poor drainage:** danger of air entering arterial return. Alert perfusionist/surgeon, make pump flow safe under the circuit emergency protocol, inspect venous cannula kinks/malposition, air lock, vacuum or obstruction; assess true volume before giving fluid.
- **High arterial-line pressure with low patient flow:** suspect kink/obstruction, arterial cannula malposition or **aortic dissection/false-lumen perfusion**. Do not simply raise pump speed; check upstream/downstream pressures, patient arterial pressures, NIRS, cannula and aorta urgently.
- **Air detected in arterial circuit:** coordinated **stop/prevent further air delivery**, secure and de-air circuit per perfusion protocol, identify source and restore safe perfusion promptly; surgeon assesses coronary/cerebral air-management options.
- Also recognise **oxygenator gas failure/clotting**: verify gas supply, sweep/FiO₂, circuit anticoagulation and need for component exchange.

> **Closing point:** Call the perfusionist and surgeon immediately; protect the patient and the circuit together.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: How is anaesthetic depth maintained on CPB, and why can awareness occur?
items.q: How is anaesthetic depth maintained on CPB, and why can awareness occur?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- With pulmonary blood flow/ventilation reduced, volatile agent delivered to the **ordinary breathing circuit may no longer reach the patient**. Provide vaporised agent through an appropriate **oxygenator vapour system with scavenging**, or a verified **IV hypnotic infusion**.
- Reconfirm delivery when CPB begins and whenever infusions/lines change; monitor reservoir/oxygenator settings and perfusion transitions.
- CPB causes **haemodilution, altered protein binding, circuit sequestration, hypothermia and rewarming-related pharmacokinetic changes**.
- Neuromuscular blockade prevents movement but not awareness; **BIS/processed EEG may be falsely reassuring during profound hypothermia** and cannot replace a reliable drug-delivery plan.

> **Closing point:** The anaesthetic route must follow the blood, not the ventilator.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: How much heparin is given for bypass and how is it monitored?
items.q: How much heparin is given for bypass and how is it monitored?
items.a:
- 300 to 400 units/kg.
- Confirm ACT above the validated local device/circuit target **before CPB**; >480 s is common, not universal.
- ACT repeated every 20 to 30 minutes.
- Investigate an inadequate response; resistance definitions vary, often >400–500 IU/kg to reach target. Check dose/test and antithrombin.

> **Closing point:** Check the ACT before the cannulae are connected.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2023

items.title: What are the causes of heparin resistance?
items.q: What are the causes of heparin resistance?
items.a:
- Antithrombin deficiency, congenital or acquired.
- Preoperative heparin, liver disease, DIC.
- Increased heparin-binding proteins (e.g. PF4), thrombocytosis and inflammation; high factor VIII/fibrinogen can alter apparent assay response.
- Andexanet alfa can interfere with heparin-activated antithrombin; exclude dose/delivery and test error or an acute-phase assay effect.

> **Closing point:** Give antithrombin concentrate (or plasma if appropriate/unavailable) for confirmed/suspected antithrombin deficiency; investigate other causes.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2023 / CPB guideline

items.title: How do you manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia for cardiac surgery?
items.q: How do you manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia for cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Assess 4Ts/timing, PF4 immunoassay and functional testing; acute immune HIT is prothrombotic and requires avoidance of UFH/LMWH.
- If nonurgent, wait until functional assay is negative (subacute B) or antibodies absent (remote), not a fixed 100 days.
- Urgent acute/subacute A CPB: experienced-centre bivalirudin protocol; avoid circuit stasis and account for renal impairment/no reversal.
- In subacute B/remote HIT, heparin confined to CPB may be appropriate under expert guidance; use nonheparin treatment before/after and monitor platelets.

> **Closing point:** The HIT phase determines whether intraoperative heparin is acceptable.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2023

items.title: How does protamine reverse heparin and what is the dose?
items.q: How does protamine reverse heparin and what is the dose?
items.a:
- A positively charged protein forms a complex with negatively charged heparin; give slowly after successful CPB separation.
- Titrate to residual heparin where possible. **1 mg per 100 IU** is a traditional reference, not a mandatory dose for all cumulative heparin.
- Contemporary CPB guidance favours a lower ratio (<1 mg/100 IU when appropriate), guided by testing and bleeding.
- Excess protamine impairs platelets/coagulation; prolonged ACT or oozing alone does not prove residual heparin.

> **Closing point:** Exclude other causes before repeatedly adding protamine.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2023 / CPB guideline

items.title: What are the adverse effects of protamine?
items.q: What are the adverse effects of protamine?
items.a:
- Vasodilatory hypotension, pulmonary vasoconstriction/PH with RV failure, and anaphylaxis; excess dosing impairs coagulation.
- Stop infusion, support circulation/oxygenation, treat the mechanism and be ready for re-heparinisation/CPB rescue.
- Prior protamine exposure/NPH insulin use warrants attention. Fish allergy alone is not a reliable predictor or automatic contraindication.
- Heparin rebound reflects re-emergence of heparin effect and is not itself proof of a protamine allergic reaction.

> **Closing point:** Slow, titrated administration with rescue readiness.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2023

items.title: How does aortic atheroma influence aortic cannulation?
items.q: How does aortic atheroma influence aortic cannulation?
items.a:
- Risk of embolic stroke and dissection.
- Epiaortic ultrasound evaluates cannulation/clamp sites; TOE assesses accessible segments but has a distal ascending-aortic blind spot.
- Alternative cannulation: axillary, femoral or innominate.
- No-touch or off-pump techniques.

> **Closing point:** Assess the aorta before clamping.

items.title: What is cardioplegia and how is it delivered?
items.q: What is cardioplegia and how is it delivered?
items.a:
- High-potassium solution induces diastolic arrest.
- Cold or warm blood or crystalloid (St Thomas, del Nido).
- Antegrade via the aortic root; retrograde via the coronary sinus.
- Re-dosing depends on solution, route, temperature and myocardial activity: many blood regimens use 20–30 minutes; del Nido/HTK can permit longer intervals under protocol.

> **Closing point:** It lowers oxygen demand during the cross-clamp.

> **Source:** BJA Educ 2026

items.title: Choose antegrade, retrograde or selective ostial cardioplegia for different cardiac lesions.
items.q: Choose antegrade, retrograde or selective ostial cardioplegia for different cardiac lesions.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Antegrade aortic-root cardioplegia** distributes down patent coronary arteries after cross-clamping; important **coronary obstruction** may impair distal delivery.
- In **severe aortic regurgitation**, antegrade root cardioplegia may run into the LV, distend it and inadequately protect myocardium; choose **retrograde coronary-sinus** delivery and/or **direct coronary ostial** dosing once the aorta is open.
- **Retrograde** delivery can bypass proximal coronary stenoses but may be less reliable for the **RV**, and requires appropriate coronary-sinus positioning/pressure.
- **Selective ostial** delivery is useful during AVR/aortic root operations. Maintain correct temperature, dose/interval, coronary perfusion and venting; inadequate protection causes stunning, ischaemia and failure to wean.

> **Closing point:** The valve lesion and coronary anatomy determine how cardioplegia reaches the myocardium.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.q: What is the mechanism of tranexamic acid?
items.a:
- Lysine analogue that binds plasminogen.
- Blocks plasmin formation and fibrin breakdown.
- Renally cleared; dose-reduce in renal impairment.
- High doses cause seizures.

> **Closing point:** It is antifibrinolytic, not procoagulant.

items.title: Interpret common ROTEM/TEG abnormalities after CPB and give targeted treatments.
items.q: Interpret common ROTEM/TEG abnormalities after CPB and give targeted treatments.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [Blue Book 2025: Goal-directed bleeding management, pp59–79](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_Blue_Book_PDF.pdf?language=en) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://www.eacts.org/clinical-practice-guideline/2024-eacts-eactaic-guidelines-on-patient-blood-management-in-adult-cardiac-surgery-in-collaboration-with-ebcp/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- First consider **surgical bleeding, temperature, pH, calcium** and residual heparin; viscoelastic tests complement rather than replace the operative assessment.
- **Prolonged EXTEM clotting time** may indicate **coagulation-factor deficit** (consider protocol-guided plasma/PCC), but compare with heparin-sensitive channels and standard tests before treating.
- A **heparin effect** is suggested when **INTEM is abnormal but HEPTEM corrects** (or the equivalent heparinase comparison): reassess heparin/protamine balance.
- **Low FIBTEM clot amplitude/MCF** supports fibrinogen deficiency → fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate under protocol.
- **Low EXTEM clot firmness with relatively preserved FIBTEM** points toward platelet-number/function contribution → consider platelets according to labs/clinical bleeding.
- **Excess lysis** suggests hyperfibrinolysis → TXA when appropriate. Local **A5/A10/MCF thresholds vary by assay and centre**; routine channels can miss P2Y12-related dysfunction.

> **Closing point:** Match the faulty clot component to treatment rather than giving every product indiscriminately.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What do TRICS III and ATACAS mean for cardiac-surgical blood conservation?
items.q: What do TRICS III and ATACAS mean for cardiac-surgical blood conservation?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://www.eacts.org/clinical-practice-guideline/2024-eacts-eactaic-guidelines-on-patient-blood-management-in-adult-cardiac-surgery-in-collaboration-with-ebcp/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **TRICS III:** in moderate/high-risk cardiac surgery, a **restrictive RBC threshold around Hb 75 g/L** was **non-inferior** to a liberal strategy for a major composite of death, MI, stroke and new dialysis (11.4% vs 12.5%). It is not a rule for unstable haemorrhage or active ischaemia.
- **ATACAS:** **tranexamic acid** reduced blood-product use and reoperation for bleeding/tamponade, but increased **seizures**; no significant primary composite thrombotic/death benefit. Choose dose using renal function, seizure risk and local protocol.
- Practical application: use a **patient-blood-management programme**, treat surgical bleeding and specific coagulation deficits, and interpret the trial population before changing care.

> **Closing point:** Restrictive transfusion is contextual, and TXA benefits must be weighed against dose-related harm.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What is the rationale for deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.q: What is the rationale for deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.a:
- Cerebral protection when circulation stops.
- Cerebral metabolic rate falls about 6 to 7% per degree Celsius.
- Gives a bloodless field for arch surgery at 18 to 20 °C.
- No guaranteed safe arrest time; neurological risk rises with duration. Selective cerebral perfusion provides additional protection and may permit warmer arrest.

> **Closing point:** The aim is brain protection.

> **Source:** Exam report 2019.2

items.title: What are the consequences of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.q: What are the consequences of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.a:
- Neurological injury: stroke, delirium, seizures, cognitive decline.
- Coagulopathy: platelet dysfunction, fibrinolysis.
- Arrhythmias on cooling and rewarming; renal and visceral injury.
- Hyperglycaemia and inflammatory response.

> **Closing point:** Not the same as cardioplegia or ECMO.

> **Source:** Exam report 2019.2

items.title: What are the problems with rewarming after bypass?
items.q: What are the problems with rewarming after bypass?
items.a:
- Rewarm slowly; outflow temperature at most 37 °C.
- Cerebral hyperthermia and gas emboli.
- After-drop, shivering, vasodilation and bleeding.
- Target nasopharyngeal 36 to 37 °C before separation.

> **Closing point:** Avoid overshooting.

items.title: What are the cardiac effects of hypothermia?
items.q: What are the cardiac effects of hypothermia?
items.a:
- Bradycardia and conduction slowing (J waves).
- Ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility rises with deeper cooling; no fixed temperature guarantees VF or safety.
- Reduced oxygen demand and better protection.
- Arrhythmias on rewarming.

> **Closing point:** Cooling protects but makes the heart unstable.

items.title: Which factors determine the success of cardioversion in AF?
items.q: Which factors determine the success of cardioversion in AF?
items.a:
- Duration of AF and left atrial size.
- Underlying structural disease and reversible causes.
- Electrolytes, amiodarone pre-treatment.
- Appropriate biphasic energy, good pad contact/impedance and effective vector (AL or AP); synchronise to the R wave.

> **Closing point:** Answer both success and safety.

> **Source:** Exam report 2017.1

items.title: What makes cardioversion safe?
items.q: What makes cardioversion safe?
items.a:
- **Preop:** assess AF duration/onset, thromboembolic risk, anticoagulant adherence and underlying disease; correct electrolytes and exclude digoxin toxicity.
- For elective AF >24 h/uncertain onset (ESC 2024): ≥3 weeks therapeutic anticoagulation or TOE-guided early cardioversion with anticoagulation. Thrombus means defer/treat/re-image.
- **Intraop:** monitored short anaesthetic, airway/resuscitation readiness and synchronised shock; plan for bradycardia, VF, hypotension and burns. Instability needs rescue without waiting for anticoagulation.
- **Postop:** usually ≥4 weeks anticoagulation despite a clear TOE, then long-term by stroke risk; monitor recovery and ECG.

> **Closing point:** Restore rhythm safely and prevent embolism.

> **Source:** Exam report 2017.1

items.title: What is the role of cardioversion for intraoperative arrhythmias?
items.q: What is the role of cardioversion for intraoperative arrhythmias?
items.a:
- First line for unstable tachyarrhythmia.
- Patient already anaesthetised; defibrillator at hand.
- Correct causes concurrently; do not delay emergency cardioversion for an unstable tachyarrhythmia. Pulseless/polymorphic VT or VF needs unsynchronised shock.
- Not for automatic rhythms such as sinus tachycardia.

> **Closing point:** Use drugs for stable arrhythmias.

items.title: What is internal defibrillation?
items.q: What is internal defibrillation?
items.a:
- Sterile paddles applied directly to the heart with an open chest.
- 10 to 20 J biphasic.
- Safe energy is lower than external because impedance is bypassed.
- Used in theatre or after resternotomy.

> **Closing point:** Open chest, low energy.

items.title: What changes in the arrest algorithm after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What changes in the arrest algorithm after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Witnessed monitored VF/pVT with defibrillator immediately ready: up to three **rapid** stacked shocks, initial sequence within approximately one minute; otherwise CPR without delay.
- In asystole/extreme bradycardia, exclude hidden VF, try epicardial pacing rapidly and confirm mechanical capture; CPR if ineffective.
- Prepare trained emergency resternotomy **within 5 minutes** if not rapidly reversed; address tamponade, haemorrhage and other reversible causes.
- Avoid routine 1 mg adrenaline boluses; use CALS-ANZ specialist drug strategy, including amiodarone for refractory VF/pVT.

> **Closing point:** The stacked-shock exception must never create prolonged no-flow.

items.title: What are the major complications of percutaneous coronary intervention?
items.q: What are the major complications of percutaneous coronary intervention?
items.a:
- Coronary perforation and tamponade.
- Vessel closure, no-reflow and infarction.
- Arrhythmia, access-site bleeding and retroperitoneal haematoma.
- Contrast reaction, AKI and stroke.

> **Closing point:** Know them before the call comes.

items.title: How do you manage coronary perforation?
items.q: How do you manage coronary perforation?
items.a:
- Coordinate with interventionalist/surgeon; weigh protamine reversal against fresh-stent/catheter thrombosis while controlling the perforation.
- Balloon tamponade, covered stent.
- Pericardiocentesis for tamponade.
- Surgical repair if refractory.

> **Closing point:** Call the surgeon early.

items.title: What are the complications of TAVI?
items.q: What are the complications of TAVI?
items.a:
- Vascular injury, annular rupture, coronary obstruction.
- Aortic dissection, valve embolisation, paravalvular leak.
- Conduction block needing a pacemaker.
- Stroke and tamponade.

> **Closing point:** Surgical standby is essential.

items.title: What are the complications of AF ablation?
items.q: What are the complications of AF ablation?
items.a:
- Tamponade/perforation; incidence varies with technique and centre.
- Stroke or air embolism.
- Atrio-oesophageal fistula (delayed).
- Phrenic nerve injury and pulmonary vein stenosis.

> **Closing point:** With delayed fever, chest pain or neurological symptoms after ablation, urgently consider atrio-oesophageal fistula; avoid oesophageal instrumentation if suspected.

> **Source:** Blue Book 2021

items.title: Why is the catheter laboratory a high-risk location for anaesthesia?
items.q: Why is the catheter laboratory a high-risk location for anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Remote site with limited access and radiation.
- Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy.
- Unfamiliar team and equipment.
- Need for surgical and perfusion back-up.

> **Closing point:** Plan for crisis before the case starts.

items.title: 1. Systolic anterior motion and hypotension after mitral repair
items.q: After mitral valve repair, hypotension worsens as adrenaline is increased. TOE reveals a very small hyperdynamic LV, systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet and posteriorly directed MR. Explain the diagnosis and management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · Expanded Set 13 notes (chapters listed in model answer).

## Diagnosis and mechanism

- This is **dynamic left-ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) due to SAM after mitral repair**, not simply low contractility. Repair geometry can bring the anterior leaflet/coaptation point towards the septum.
- A small underfilled **hyperdynamic LV** generates high systolic flow velocity/drag, drawing the anterior leaflet into the LVOT, generating **dynamic obstruction** and often **posteriorly directed MR**.
- Beta-agonists increase contractility and LVOT velocity; vasodilation reduces afterload; tachycardia and low preload decrease LV cavity size. **More adrenaline can make pressure and forward flow worse.**

## Differentiate from alternatives

- TOE: look for anterior leaflet motion against the septum, a dynamic LVOT Doppler gradient (often late-peaking), MR direction, LV cavity size, regional wall-motion abnormalities and ventricular function.
- **Afterload mismatch** after eliminating severe MR can cause low output, but typically shows **depressed LV systolic function**, not a tiny vigorous ventricle with SAM. Exclude residual primary MR, prosthesis/repair dysfunction, coronary air/ischaemia, RV failure, bleeding and tamponade.

## Immediate management

- **1.** **Call surgeon and perfusionist**, reassess TOE and the valve repair while maintaining coronary/systemic perfusion.
- **2.** **Reduce or stop positive inotropy** driving obstruction, if haemodynamics permit. Avoid inappropriate vasodilators.
- **3.** **Restore SVR/afterload** with titrated **phenylephrine or vasopressin** (other vasopressors depending on physiology); this opposes dynamic obstruction. Assess coronary perfusion.
- **4.** **Correct genuine LV underfilling cautiously** with a targeted volume challenge; avoid reflexive fluid loading if other signs suggest congestion.
- **5.** Control tachycardia; consider cautious **short-acting beta-blockade once perfusion pressure is supported** and under TOE/arterial monitoring.
- **6.** If severe obstruction persists or repair geometry is responsible, **surgical revision** may be necessary; reinstitute CPB if unable to stabilise.

## Postoperative plan

Document mechanism and the final TOE gradient/MR, avoid triggers and hand over a clear haemodynamic and rhythm strategy to ICU.

**Evidence:** Expanded Set 13 notes, chapters 3, 7 and worked Case B; cardiac valve/CPB guidance.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies SAM-related dynamic LVOTO rather than assuming contractile failure
- Explains why low preload/SVR, tachycardia and beta-agonists worsen obstruction
- Distinguishes SAM from afterload mismatch and other post-repair causes using TOE
- Stops/reduces inappropriate inotropy and restores SVR
- Uses a cautious assessed fluid challenge and rate control when appropriate
- Escalates to surgical review/revision or CPB if refractory
- Gives an ICU handover and reassessment plan

items.title: 2. CPB circuit crisis: rising line pressure, falling reservoir and NIRS
items.q: During established CPB, the arterial circuit pressure rises, venous reservoir level falls and cerebral NIRS decreases. Describe the differential, immediate safety actions and troubleshooting with the surgeon and perfusionist.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · Expanded Set 13 notes (chapters listed in model answer).

## Recognise two simultaneous threats

- **Low venous reservoir** implies venous drainage into the reservoir is less than pump outflow and threatens **air entrainment** into arterial return.
- **High arterial-line pressure** with poor patient perfusion suggests **outflow obstruction**, arterial cannula malposition/kink, clamp/filter obstruction or **aortic dissection/false-lumen perfusion**.
- Falling **NIRS** may represent cerebral malperfusion from inadequate pump flow/DO₂, abnormal PaCO₂, arch-vessel obstruction or sensor artefact; it is not automatically isolated hypotension.

## Immediate coordinated response

- **1.** **Declare a circuit/perfusion emergency.** Surgeon, perfusionist and anaesthetist use closed-loop communication. Protect the patient and maintain a safe circuit; the **perfusionist adjusts/stops/clamps flow according to the emergency protocol**. Do not blindly speed the pump up or permit an empty reservoir.
- **2.** Establish whether the high pressure is **proximal circuit pressure** versus actual systemic arterial MAP. Check pump displayed flow, inlet/outlet and arterial line pressures, bilateral arterial pressure if available, oxygenator status, reservoir and air-detector alarms.
- **3.** Assess systemic and cerebral perfusion: patient pressure, NIRS both sides, Hb/haematocrit, SvO₂, ABG, oxygenator outlet saturation, temperature, PaCO₂ and lactate. Verify the NIRS sensor and a functioning oxygen source.

## Find and correct the venous drainage problem

- Inspect cannula seating, kinking, air-lock/obstructed SVC/IVC, patient position, venous tubing and excessive/inadequate vacuum-assisted drainage.
- Determine if true volume depletion is present; **reposition or correct obstruction before reflex massive fluid administration**. Maintain reservoir safety while drainage is restored.

## Find and correct the arterial outflow problem

- Check arterial cannula position and line clamps/kinks, filter/oxygenator obstruction and aortic pressure. Consider **iatrogenic aortic dissection** or false-lumen cannulation if high circuit pressure coexists with low patient perfusion and falling NIRS; prompt **TOE/direct surgical assessment** and re-cannulation may be necessary.
- If arterial air is suspected, follow the **air emergency protocol** to prevent further delivery, de-air and rapidly re-establish safe organ perfusion.

## Prevent recurrence
