Reconfirm proper cannulation and perfusion flow/DO₂, oxygenator function, cerebral monitoring, ACT and clear emergency roles before resuming routine bypass management. Document the event and monitor neurological/organ effects after rewarming.

**Evidence:** Expanded Set 13 notes, chapter 4, 'Three dangerous technical emergencies on CPB'.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises low reservoir/air-entry threat and high arterial pressure/low-flow threat
- Calls perfusionist and surgeon and follows the circuit emergency protocol
- Does not blindly increase pump speed or permit an empty reservoir
- Troubleshoots venous cannula, obstruction, vacuum and volume status
- Considers arterial cannula obstruction, malposition and aortic dissection
- Investigates NIRS decline with true perfusion, DO₂, gas exchange and technical checks
- Explains safe restoration, documentation and neurological surveillance

items.title: 3. Vasoplegia after bypass in a patient on an ACE inhibitor
items.q: A 68-year-old man on an ACE inhibitor has a good ejection fraction on TOE but a MAP of 48 mmHg, cardiac index 4.2 and SVR 450 after separation from bypass for CABG. Explain the pathophysiology and outline your management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [2024 EACTS perioperative medication guideline](https://academic.oup.com/ejcts/article/67/1/ezae355/7815986)

## Recognition

**Vasoplegia** is excessive vasodilation with normal/high cardiac output, low SVR and vasopressor-dependent hypotension. Vasoplegic shock adds tissue hypoperfusion; incidence and prognosis vary substantially with definition, severity and case mix, so do not memorise an unqualified mortality percentage. Exclude hypovolaemia/bleeding, tamponade, LV/RV failure, protamine reaction (if given), anaphylaxis, infection and drug effects using the clinical time course, TOE, pressures, lactate and perfusion.

## Pathophysiology

CPB contact activation triggers a **systemic inflammatory response** (complement, cytokines), inducing nitric oxide synthase and increased **nitric oxide–cGMP**, with potassium channel (KATP) opening in vascular smooth muscle, and **vasopressin deficiency** (depleted stores) and catecholamine hyporesponsiveness. Risk factors: **ACE inhibitors or ARBs**, calcium channel blockers, amiodarone, beta-blockers, preoperative heart failure with low EF, long CPB time, diabetes, endocarditis and previous cardiac surgery.

## Management: multimodal vasopressors

- **1.** Optimise **preload** (volume from the pump) and exclude other causes.
- **2.** **Noradrenaline** first; add **vasopressin** (commonly 0.01–0.04 units/min under local protocol; higher doses require specialist judgement because of ischaemia risk), which is catecholamine-sparing and has little effect on PVR.
- **3.** Escalate with **methylene blue** (1 to 2 mg/kg IV over 15 to 30 minutes), which inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase; caution with serotonergic drugs (serotonin syndrome), G6PD deficiency, and pulmonary hypertension; it turns urine green and can distort pulse oximetry.
- **4.** **Hydrocortisone** may be considered for refractory shock with suspected adrenal insufficiency or a relevant septic-shock indication (e.g. 200 mg/day). Evidence for routine use specifically in isolated post-CPB vasoplegia is limited; it is not an obligatory next treatment.
- **5.** **Angiotensin II** (ATHOS-3 trial in vasodilatory shock) and **hydroxocobalamin** are rescue options; adrenaline if there is also low output.
- **6.** Correct acidosis, calcium and temperature.

**Monitor response:** MAP (often initially ≥65 mmHg, individualised), lactate trend, urine output, cardiac output and peripheral perfusion; prevent excessive vasoconstriction/ischaemia. **Preop prevention:** optimise volume and anticipate high-risk cases. ACEI/ARB management is individualised: the 2024 EACTS medication guideline permits consideration of continuation, whereas some anaesthetic pathways omit them. If held, use indication, haemodynamics and drug half-life rather than a universal 24-hour rule. Limit avoidable CPB/inflammatory burden.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines vasoplegia (low SVR, high output) and excludes other causes
- Explains the inflammatory, nitric oxide and vasopressin-deficiency mechanisms
- Lists risk factors (ACE inhibitors, long bypass, poor LV)
- Uses noradrenaline first, then vasopressin
- Describes methylene blue (dose, cautions)
- Distinguishes selected rescue agents from routine therapy and recognises limited steroid evidence
- Includes prevention and monitoring

items.title: 4. Acute RV failure when weaning after mitral valve replacement
items.q: As you wean a patient from cardiopulmonary bypass after mitral valve replacement, the right ventricle dilates, the CVP rises to 24 and the systolic pressure falls. Explain the mechanisms and your management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [Blue Book 2021: RV dysfunction pp115–124; VAD noncardiac surgery pp125–134; AF ablation chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book_2021-Version8.pdf?language=en) · [POQI consensus: perioperative management of the vulnerable/failing RV (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13741-024-00397-5)

## Why the RV fails

Risk factors: pre-existing RV dysfunction or **pulmonary hypertension**, long CPB, inadequate RV myocardial protection, LVAD insertion or heart transplantation, and **air or graft problems in the right coronary artery** (the ostium is anterior, so air collects there). **Protamine** can cause pulmonary vasoconstriction. After CPB, PVR rises with atelectasis, reperfusion injury and inflammatory mediators. The thin-walled RV tolerates volume but not afterload; dilation leads to a spiral of falling RV coronary perfusion, septal shift (ventricular interdependence) and falling LV filling.

## Diagnosis

Diagnose **a syndrome**, not a single CVP cutoff: low output/hypotension with a dilated poorly contracting RV, septal flattening/leftward shift, impaired LV filling and often functional TR. CVP is often high and may approach/exceed PCWP; PA pressure may be elevated with PH or fall when a failing RV cannot generate flow. PAC trends and direct inspection complement TOE. A fused c–v wave suggests TR, not proof of primary RV failure. RV:LV dimensions and TAPSE/FAC are supportive, but isolated TAPSE is load-dependent and often reduced after pericardiotomy. Check mitral prosthesis function, LV function, coronary air/ischaemia, tamponade and RVOT obstruction; an RV-to-PA pressure gradient with Doppler helps identify the latter.

## Management in order

- **1.** **Preload:** assess filling with TOE and haemodynamics. If underfilled, give a small titrated fluid/pump-blood challenge. If genuinely overdistended/congested, controlled unloading into the CPB circuit may help while supported; later consider diuresis/ultrafiltration. Do not give nitrates, head-up positioning or remove volume solely because CVP is high in an already hypotensive patient.
- **2.** **Rhythm and AV synchrony:** pace or cardiovert; atrial wires if hypertrophied.
- **3.** **Perfusion pressure:** noradrenaline and/or low-dose vasopressin to preserve systemic and RV coronary perfusion. Vasopressin is useful when PVR is high; avoid excessive doses of any vasopressor. Pure phenylephrine can increase PVR and reduce output. There is no universal requirement to use vasopressin before noradrenaline.
- **4.** **Contractility:** titrated dobutamine, adrenaline or milrinone according to pressure, ischaemia and rhythm, often with vasopressor support because inodilators reduce SVR. The 2021 Blue Book discusses intratracheal milrinone, but that is limited-evidence specialist practice, not a standard first-line rescue dose to reproduce in a generic answer.
- **5.** **Afterload:** FiO2 1.0, normocapnia, avoid high PEEP and tidal volumes, normal pH; **inhaled nitric oxide** (10 to 40 ppm) or inhaled iloprost or epoprostenol, with IV agents if inadequate.
- **6.** If severe/refractory, **restore CPB support early** and correct the surgical/physiological cause. Select RVAD or VA-ECMO by isolated RV versus biventricular/respiratory failure. IABP can help associated LV failure/ischaemia or coronary perfusion, but supplies no direct RV flow and must not delay appropriate RV support.

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists risk factors (pre-existing RV disease, PH, long CPB, right coronary air, protamine)
- Explains afterload sensitivity and interdependence
- Describes haemodynamic and TOE diagnosis
- Optimises preload (give or remove), rhythm and AV synchrony
- Chooses vasopressin or cautious noradrenaline and avoids phenylephrine
- Uses dobutamine or adrenaline for contractility
- Uses inhaled pulmonary vasodilators and ventilatory strategy
- Escalates early to CPB and selects RVAD/VA-ECMO; understands the limited role of IABP in isolated RV failure

items.title: 5. HeartMate 3 LVAD for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
items.q: A 58-year-old man with a HeartMate 3 left ventricular assist device presents for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Outline the physiology of the device and your perioperative management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [Blue Book 2021: RV dysfunction pp115–124; VAD noncardiac surgery pp125–134; AF ablation chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book_2021-Version8.pdf?language=en) · [ARIES-HM3 primary RCT, JAMA 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37950897/) · [THANZ updated warfarin reversal recommendations, MJA 2025](https://www.mja.com.au/journal/2025/222/1/updated-recommendations-warfarin-reversal-setting-four-factor-prothrombin) · [AHA scientific statement: periprocedural CIED management (2024)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12068544/)

## Device physiology

HeartMate 3 is a **fully magnetically levitated centrifugal continuous-flow LVAD**. Blood enters at the LV apex and returns through an **outflow graft** to the ascending aorta. The percutaneous **driveline carries electrical power/control**, not blood. HeartMate II is an older axial-flow device; HeartWare HVAD is a legacy centrifugal device withdrawn from new implantation in 2021, and should not be equated with HM3.

Flow depends on RV-mediated LV filling, pump speed and the pressure gradient across the pump. Hypovolaemia or RV failure reduces flow; hypertension raises afterload and reduces flow. Little/no palpable pulse may be normal: standard cuffs and pulse oximetry may fail. Complications include acquired von Willebrand dysfunction/GI bleeding, infection, stroke, RV failure, arrhythmia, aortic regurgitation, obstruction and pump thrombosis.

## Preop

- Agree urgency, location and rescue plan with surgeon, VAD coordinator and heart-failure team. Review device model/settings, alarms, dependence, functional capacity, recent echo/RV function, haemolysis/infection, FBC, renal function, INR and current drugs. Identify the driveline route before port placement.
- **Antithrombotics are device- and patient-specific.** HM3 usually requires a vitamin K antagonist (commonly INR 2–3, confirm centre target), but aspirin is no longer automatically required. **ARIES-HM3 (2023):** aspirin avoidance with VKA was noninferior for the composite haemocompatibility endpoint and reduced nonsurgical bleeding (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51–0.85), without increased thromboembolism. Do not extrapolate this to every older LVAD or a separate coronary indication.
- For an elective procedure needing warfarin interruption, plan timing (often approximately 5 days) and INR testing; **bridging is individualised** to thrombosis history, device and bleeding risk, not mandatory for every HM3. Minor low-bleeding-risk procedures may not require interruption.
- Major/life-threatening warfarin bleeding needs rapid **4-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K** under the current reversal protocol, with urgent VAD/haematology input. Urgent surgery without major bleeding requires an individual reversal/re-anticoagulation plan; do not apply the old blanket “never vitamin K” advice.
- Interrogate any CIED. Disable ICD tachytherapy for anticipated EMI; use asynchronous pacing if pacing-dependent and EMI risk warrants it. Magnet behaviour differs between pacemakers and ICDs. Apply external pads and plan restoration after surgery.

## Intraop

- Have a trained VAD operator, controller, backup power/batteries and clear alarm plan. Monitor speed, power, estimated flow and pulsatility; estimated pump flow is not a direct cardiac-output measurement.
- For laparoscopic cholecystectomy use standard anaesthetic monitoring plus an arterial line (ultrasound may be needed). Doppler BP can help; its opening pressure is not always true MAP in a pulsatile patient. Consider TOE/CVC when the operation or RV disease warrants them; NIRS is an adjunct, not mandatory in every case. Use blood gases if oximetry is unreliable.
- Titrate induction/maintenance to preserve venous return, RV contractility and systemic perfusion. Maintain an individual MAP, often approximately **65–80 mmHg**, avoiding hypertension and hypoperfusion; avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressure. Neuraxial techniques are commonly unsuitable because of anticoagulation/haemodynamic risk; analgesic blocks depend on bleeding-risk guidance.
- Use low-pressure pneumoperitoneum and gradual insufflation; watch position-related preload changes and RV afterload. Protect the driveline and avoid placing ports over it.
- A suction/low-flow alarm may reflect hypovolaemia, RV failure, tamponade, arrhythmia, outflow obstruction or excessive pump speed. Assess patient, controller and echo; treat the cause, give volume only if underfilled and let the VAD team guide speed adjustment.
- **Collapse/arrest:** assess consciousness, breathing, MAP/arterial trace, capillary perfusion and device function. Absent pulse alone is not arrest. Check power/connections immediately; if perfusion is absent/inadequate, commence resuscitation including chest compressions according to the VAD arrest protocol while arranging specialist rescue. Do not withhold indicated CPR through fear of cannula displacement.

## Postop

Choose monitored recovery/HDU/ICU according to procedure and physiology. Confirm device function and CIED settings/ICD therapies, monitor RV failure, bleeding, infection, haemolysis and organ perfusion. Restart warfarin and any indicated bridging/antiplatelet treatment when haemostasis permits, with explicit VAD-team targets and follow-up.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes continuous-flow LVAD physiology and loss of pulse
- Preload and afterload dependence; RV function
- Individualises warfarin interruption/bridging; explains ARIES-HM3 and major-bleeding reversal with PCC plus vitamin K
- ICD or pacemaker reprogramming and pads
- Monitoring: arterial line, NIRS, TOE and VAD controller
- Maintains MAP, preload and low PVR; limits laparoscopy pressure
- Plans for arrest and VAD alarms
- Explains the outflow graft versus electrical driveline and HM3-specific aspirin evidence
- Gives a postoperative device/antithrombotic plan

items.title: 6. IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO in post-infarct cardiogenic shock
items.q: Compare the intra-aortic balloon pump, a percutaneous microaxial pump (Impella) and venoarterial ECMO in the management of cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: Management of cardiogenic shock after ACS (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140595/) · [DanGer-Shock primary RCT, NEJM 2024](https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572) · [ECLS-SHOCK primary RCT, NEJM 2023](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227) · [IABP-SHOCK II primary RCT, NEJM 2012](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1208410)

## Principle

Mechanical circulatory support is a **bridge** to recovery, revascularisation, decision or durable support/transplant, chosen by shock severity and LV/RV/respiratory physiology. Activate a shock team and treat the cause, including prompt revascularisation and repair of mechanical complications. Adequate early support matters; choose the device that achieves perfusion goals with an acceptable complication burden rather than automatically choosing the smallest device.

| Device | Support and effect | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IABP** | Diastolic augmentation and presystolic unloading; modest, variable assistance without independent pump flow | Relatively small access; selected acute MR/VSD or perioperative LV-ischaemia bridges; possible adjunct to ECMO unloading | Requires native ejection; timing is harder with tachyarrhythmia but AF is not an absolute contraindication; avoid significant AR/dissection and unsuitable vascular anatomy |
| **Impella** (microaxial LVAD) | LV-to-aorta pump that directly unloads the LV; flow depends on model and loading (CP approximately 3–4 L/min; 5.5 up to 5.5 L/min) | Greater LV unloading than IABP; does not require ECG triggering | Requires adequate RV filling; no oxygenation support. Bleeding, haemolysis, vascular/limb injury; important exclusions include LV thrombus, mechanical aortic valve and significant AR; assess AS/anatomy and device suitability |
| **VA-ECMO** | Venous drainage, oxygenation and arterial return; circuit-dependent high flow, often 3–5 L/min in an adult | Biventricular/cardiopulmonary support and selected ECPR | Peripheral arterial return raises LV afterload: monitor aortic valve opening, LV distension, stasis and pulmonary oedema. Assess need for unloading; it is not automatic in every patient. Differential upper-body hypoxaemia, bleeding, thrombosis, stroke and limb ischaemia |

## Selection

- Isolated LV failure with adequate RV: IABP or Impella.
- Biventricular failure, severe hypoxia or arrest: VA-ECMO (± LV unloading).
- ECMO needs a reversible lesion or a destination; a nonrecoverable condition without an exit strategy or severe irreversible neurological injury may preclude it. Age, frailty and comorbidity affect candidacy but are not universal absolute cutoffs.

## Anaesthetic relevance

Anticoagulation, bleeding, transport, TOE (position and LV size), and combined strategies.

## Trial evidence: distinguish device and population

- **IABP-SHOCK II (2012):** 30-day mortality 39.7% versus 41.3% with usual care (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.79–1.17; P=0.69). It does not support routine IABP in AMI shock; it does not settle every mechanical-complication/postcardiotomy indication.
- **DanGer-Shock (2024):** selected STEMI-related shock patients treated with Impella CP had lower 180-day mortality, 45.8% versus 58.5% (HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.55–0.99; P=0.04), but more adverse events and renal replacement. This cannot be generalised to all shock, predominant RV failure or severely neurologically injured postarrest patients.
- **ECLS-SHOCK (2023):** routine early ECLS in infarct-related shock did not reduce 30-day mortality (47.8% versus 49.0%; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.80–1.19; P=0.81) and increased bleeding/vascular complications. Selective salvage or postcardiotomy ECMO is a different clinical question.

After insertion, reassess lactate, urine output, haemodynamics, echo, cannula position, perfusion/haemolysis and bleeding; define an escalation and weaning/exit plan.

## Self-marking checklist

- States MCS as a bridge and the least-support principle
- IABP: mechanism, augmentation and limits
- Impella: mechanism, output and complications
- VA-ECMO: support, increased afterload, differential hypoxia
- Selects device by RV function, oxygenation and goal
- Assesses the need for selective LV unloading during ECMO
- Accurately contrasts IABP-SHOCK II, DanGer-Shock and ECLS-SHOCK without extrapolating across populations

items.title: 7. Worsening hypoxaemia on VV-ECMO during sepsis
items.q: An adult with severe ARDS on VV-ECMO becomes more hypoxaemic during sepsis (SpO₂ 82%), despite increasing sweep-gas flow. Cardiac output has risen substantially. Explain the physiology and describe your troubleshooting and treatment.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: VV ECMO in severe acute respiratory failure (2024), indexed record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38481419/) · [ELSO adult VV-ECMO guideline (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8315725/) · Expanded Set 13 notes (chapters listed in model answer).

## Why a higher sweep has not fixed oxygenation

- **VV-ECMO provides gas exchange but no direct circulatory support**. Oxygenated ECMO return mixes with the native venous return, and the lungs may remain profoundly shunting.
- Systemic SaO₂ depends heavily on **effective ECMO blood flow / native cardiac output**, native lung oxygenation, Hb, oxygenator performance, oxygen consumption and recirculation.
- In **sepsis with high cardiac output**, a fixed ECMO blood flow represents a smaller fraction of venous return; more blood bypasses the oxygenator and passes through poorly functioning native lungs, so saturation may fall.
- **Sweep gas principally removes CO₂**. Once oxygenator gas supply/FiO₂ and O₂ transfer are sufficient, raising sweep alone has little effect on oxygenation; a rapid PaCO₂ drop may have cerebral consequences.

## Assessment

- **1.** Confirm perfusion is adequate rather than treating an SpO₂ number in isolation: ABG, arterial content/Hb, lactate, SvO₂ and clinical tissue perfusion; check probe artefact.
- **2.** Check **ECMO circuit blood flow**, drainage pressures/chatter, pre- and post-oxygenator saturations/gases, sweep/blender oxygen source, membrane/clot/haemolysis and temperatures.
- **3.** Check **cannula position and recirculation** (oxygenated return sucked back into drainage), especially after movement; assess by imaging/echo and drainage/return saturation trends.
- **4.** Assess **native lungs** (new pneumothorax, mucus plugging, ventilator disconnection, atelectasis, pneumonia, pulmonary oedema), changes in **CO and oxygen consumption** (fever, agitation, sepsis), and anaemia.

## Treatment

- Treat sepsis and fever, manage agitation/shivering and oxygen demand, and optimise lung-protective ventilation/PEEP, prone therapy or recruitment where appropriate.
- Restore adequate effective **ECMO blood flow** within cannula/haemolysis limits, correct recirculation or cannula malposition, and address oxygenator failure/gas-supply problems.
- Optimise Hb/oxygen content according to bleeding and DO₂; avoid automatic transfusion solely to normalise SpO₂.
- Use sweep primarily to target **PaCO₂/pH**, not as a reflex correction for low SaO₂. Reassess oxygen delivery, haemodynamics and overall trajectory with the ECMO team.

**Evidence:** Expanded Set 13 notes, chapter 9 and worked Case D; ECMO physiology references.

## Self-marking checklist

- Explains effective ECMO flow/native cardiac output ratio and mixing physiology
- Distinguishes sweep-gas CO₂ clearance from blood-flow-dependent oxygenation
- Checks patient perfusion, Hb, ABG, CO, fever and oxygen consumption
- Checks circuit flow, gas delivery and membrane/oxygenator performance
- Assesses cannula migration and recirculation
- Excludes native-lung deterioration and ventilator problems
- Corrects cause and effective flow without automatic sweep escalation or unnecessary transfusion

items.title: 8. Complications in the first 24 hours after cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the common complications in the first 24 hours after cardiac surgery and their management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [ERAS Cardiac/ERAS/STS joint consensus, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38284956/) · [Blue Book 2025: Goal-directed bleeding management, pp59–79](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_Blue_Book_PDF.pdf?language=en) · [ANZCOR 11.10: cardiac surgery/CALS-ANZ (current 2026 page)](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances) · [BJA Education: Perioperative care in cardiac surgery (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8446225/)

## Haemodynamic

- **Low cardiac output:** stunning, ischaemia (graft failure), tamponade, hypovolaemia, RV failure, arrhythmia. TOE or transthoracic echo, PAC, lactate and SvO2 guide care.
- **Cardiac tamponade:** falling drain output with rising CVP, narrowed pulse pressure, hypotension; treat by **emergency resternotomy** (the ALS cardiac surgery protocol within 5 minutes of arrest).
- **Vasoplegia**, hypertension (graft protection) and ischaemia.
- **Arrhythmias:** AF in about 30% (days 2 to 3), VT/VF, heart block; correct K and Mg, amiodarone, cardioversion, epicardial pacing.

## Bleeding

Distinguish a surgical source from coagulopathy; both may coexist. Trend drainage and perfusion, check drain patency without unapproved stripping/manipulation, and call the surgeon early. Use labs and **TEG/ROTEM** to guide treatment while restoring temperature, calcium and acid–base status. Replace demonstrated platelet/fibrinogen/factor deficits and assess residual heparin versus protamine excess. TXA dosing must follow a renal-adjusted cardiac protocol: high cumulative doses increase seizure risk, and “below 100 mg/kg” is not a general safety guarantee. Ongoing brisk bleeding, instability or tamponade requires urgent surgical review/re-exploration; do not wait for an arbitrary drain threshold or quote a universal re-exploration mortality.

## Respiratory

Atelectasis, pleural effusions, pneumothorax, phrenic nerve injury, prolonged ventilation and pneumonia: early extubation when criteria are met, physiotherapy, lung-protective ventilation.

## Renal and neurological

**Acute kidney injury** (up to 30%): avoid hypotension, nephrotoxins and fluid overload; early renal replacement if indicated. **Stroke, delirium and cognitive decline:** screen, minimise sedation and benzodiazepines, maintain MAP.

## Other

Ischaemic gut, glycaemic control, infection (sternal wound), pain (multimodal opioid-sparing), and postoperative nausea.

## Self-marking checklist

- Low cardiac output with causes and TOE assessment
- Tamponade recognition and resternotomy
- Arrhythmias (AF) and management
- Bleeding: causes, coagulation testing and treatment
- Respiratory complications
- AKI and neurological complications
- Multimodal analgesia and ICU care

items.title: 9. Acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the pathophysiology, risk factors and prevention of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: Cardiac surgery-associated AKI, Feb 2026 (online Dec 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12853332/) · [PROTECTION primary RCT, NEJM 2024](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2403769) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [STS/SCA/AmSECT guideline: prevention of adult CSA-AKI (2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9891467/)

## Importance

CSA-AKI is common, with incidence depending on procedure and definition (the 2026 BJA Education review reports 5–40%); severe AKI requiring RRT is less common. **KDIGO:** creatinine increase ≥26.5 micromol/L (0.3 mg/dL) within 48 h, **or ≥1.5 times baseline within 7 days**, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h. Interpret creatinine/urine output with dilution, muscle mass, drugs and fluid balance.

## Pathophysiology

Multifactorial: **ischaemia–reperfusion** (low pressure on CPB, non-pulsatile flow), **haemolysis and free haemoglobin**, **systemic inflammation** and oxidative stress, renal microembolism, venous congestion, nephrotoxins (contrast, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin) and haemodilution. Surgical factors: long CPB or cross-clamp time, aortic manipulation.

## Risk factors

Pre-existing CKD, diabetes, age, heart failure and low EF, emergency surgery, redo surgery, anaemia, intra-aortic balloon pump, preoperative nephrotoxin exposure.

## Prevention

- **Preop:** document baseline creatinine/eGFR and risk, optimise anaemia/volume and review nephrotoxins. Balance recent contrast exposure and renal function against cardiac urgency; there is no universal 24–72-hour delay. Agree perioperative ACEI/ARB/SGLT2 inhibitor and diabetes management using the current cardiac protocol.
- **Haemodynamics:** avoid hypotension (MAP above 65 to 70, higher in chronic hypertension), avoid venous congestion and fluid overload.
- **KDIGO care bundle** (monitor creatinine and urine output, avoid nephrotoxins, optimise volume and perfusion, glycaemic control, avoid radiocontrast) and goal-directed perfusion (oxygen delivery targets on CPB).
- Minimise transfusion, limit haemolysis, avoid hydroxyethyl starch.
- **Drug evidence:** do not use low-dose dopamine, mannitol, bicarbonate or prophylactic furosemide as routine renal protection. Use diuretics for congestion, not to mask AKI. Fenoldopam is not routine: STS/SCA/AmSECT 2022 allowed selective consideration if hypotension is avoided (IIb), rather than proving benefit for all patients. Remote ischaemic preconditioning results are inconsistent.

## Management

Treat the cause, restore perfusion pressure, correct K, acid-base and fluid status, drug dosing for the renal function, and renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, overload or uraemia.

**Intraop: oxygen delivery and current evidence.** During normothermic CPB use goal-directed perfusion, with a protocol lower DO2 threshold around **280–300 mL/min/m²**, interpreted with flow, Hb, oxygen extraction and temperature; do not simply raise MAP with vasoconstrictor as a renal-protection strategy. Avoid hyperthermia/rapid rewarming and excessive haemodilution.

**PROTECTION (2024):** 3511 adults randomised to balanced IV amino acids (2 g/kg ideal body weight/day, up to 3 days) versus crystalloid placebo had creatinine-defined AKI in 26.9% versus 31.7% (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.77–0.94; P=0.002); stage 3 AKI was also less frequent. This did not establish a mortality or dialysis benefit. The 2024 CPB guideline supports considering amino acids, while the 2026 BJA review stresses the need to establish structural/long-term protection. Use within a local protocol, alongside the KDIGO bundle.

**Postop:** monitor creatinine/urine output and congestion, maintain perfusion, review drug doses/nephrotoxins and obtain nephrology input for severe/progressive AKI. RRT treats refractory metabolic/fluid complications; oliguria alone is not an automatic indication.

- **Self-test emphasis:** correctly interpret the PROTECTION outcome and avoid claiming proven mortality/dialysis benefit; explain flow/Hb/DO2 rather than MAP alone.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines CSA-AKI (KDIGO) and its burden
- Lists the mechanisms (ischaemia–reperfusion, haemolysis, inflammation)
- Lists patient and operative risk factors
- Describes preventive care (perfusion pressure, nephrotoxin avoidance, KDIGO bundle)
- Notes interventions without benefit
- Describes management and renal replacement indications
- Explains goal-directed CPB oxygen delivery and correctly qualifies PROTECTION

items.title: 10. Bleeding 400 mL/hour after CABG
items.q: A patient is bleeding 400 mL/hour from the chest drains two hours after CABG. Outline your assessment and management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [Blue Book 2025: Goal-directed bleeding management, pp59–79](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_Blue_Book_PDF.pdf?language=en) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://www.eacts.org/clinical-practice-guideline/2024-eacts-eactaic-guidelines-on-patient-blood-management-in-adult-cardiac-surgery-in-collaboration-with-ebcp/) · [FARES-II primary RCT, JAMA 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11955085/) · [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X)

## Assessment

Excessive drainage (e.g. persistently above approximately 200 mL/hour, depending on patient/procedure/local policy; the stem’s 400 mL/hour is already concerning). Is it **surgical** (anastomosis, branches, sternal edges) or **coagulopathic**? Check for **tamponade** (rising CVP, falling output, stopped drains with a haemodynamic collapse: clots can block drains), look at the drains, the chest X-ray (widening) and TOE.

## Causes of coagulopathy

Residual heparin or **inadequate protamine**, or **protamine excess**, platelet dysfunction after CPB (and antiplatelet drugs: clopidogrel, ticagrelor), **hypofibrinogenaemia**, dilution, consumption, fibrinolysis, **hypothermia, acidosis and hypocalcaemia**, and preoperative anticoagulants.

## Management

- **1.** **Resuscitate**: volume or blood, vasopressor; maintain Hb.
- **2.** **Restore physiology:** temperature above 36 °C, ionised calcium above 1.1, pH above 7.3; control hypertension (reduces suture-line stress).
- **3.** **Laboratory and viscoelastic tests (TEG/ROTEM)** and ACT or heparinase-TEG to identify residual heparin (give **additional protamine**, dosed carefully), low fibrinogen, platelets or fibrinolysis.
- **4.** **Targeted products:** platelets for relevant thrombocytopenia/dysfunction; fibrinogen concentrate/cryoprecipitate for a demonstrated deficit with bleeding (e.g. low fibrinogen/low fibrin-based clot strength; use local thresholds). Correct fibrinogen before escalating factor therapy. Consider **4-factor PCC or plasma** for factor deficiency after residual heparin is addressed. Reassess after each intervention and weigh thrombosis/volume risks. TXA follows the cardiac dosing/renal protocol; DDAVP is reserved for selected acquired platelet dysfunction/von Willebrand disease, not routine use.
- **5.** Consider **recombinant factor VIIa** only in refractory cases.
- **6.** **Return to theatre** early for tamponade, ongoing surgical bleeding or instability; do not wait.

## Principles

Algorithms based on point-of-care testing reduce transfusion; avoid unnecessary blood products (TRALI, TACO).

**FARES-II (2025):** in patients requiring coagulation-factor replacement for bleeding after CPB, 4-factor PCC produced a higher haemostatic response than frozen plasma (77.9% versus 60.4%; primary analysis n=420). This supports targeted PCC for factor-deficient bleeding, not indiscriminate PCC for every high drain output or a replacement for surgical haemostasis. Papworth is a surgical/haemostatic checklist, not a universal transfusion-threshold mandate.

## Self-marking checklist

- Differentiates surgical bleeding from coagulopathy and recognises tamponade
- Lists causes (heparin, protamine, platelet, fibrinogen, physiology)
- Restores temperature, calcium and acid-base
- Uses viscoelastic or laboratory tests
- Targets products (platelets, fibrinogen, PCC, TXA)
- Re-explores early
- Mentions limits of rescue agents and transfusion risks
- Uses targeted factor replacement and correctly applies FARES-II without delaying surgery

items.title: 11. On-pump CABG: surgical steps and anaesthetic technique
items.q: Outline the surgical steps and the anaesthetic technique for an on-pump coronary artery bypass graft in a patient with triple vessel disease and an ejection fraction of 40%.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [2024 EACTS perioperative medication guideline](https://academic.oup.com/ejcts/article/67/1/ezae355/7815986)

## Preop

Review angiography, LV function, comorbidities, drugs (continue indicated beta-blocker/statin; individualise ACEI/ARB; document aspirin/P2Y12 and anticoagulant plan), consent, anxiolysis, and Heart Team decision (SYNTAX).

**Medication detail:** continue aspirin for most CABG pathways unless a specific bleeding concern; elective P2Y12 interruption commonly uses ticagrelor 3 days, clopidogrel 5 and prasugrel 7, balanced against ACS/stent urgency. Review SGLT2 inhibitor cessation/ketone risk (typically 3 days, 4 for ertugliflozin, under local protocol), diabetes/insulin and GLP-1 aspiration-risk management; do not omit all basal insulin automatically. ACEI/ARB practice varies—document an individual plan.

## Intraop

**Surgical steps**

- **1.** **Median sternotomy**, with simultaneous harvest of conduits (left internal mammary artery, radial artery or long saphenous vein).
- **2.** **Heparinisation** (300–400 IU/kg initially, confirming the validated ACT target before CPB; >480 s is common), aortic and right atrial cannulation, and **initiation of CPB**.
- **3.** **Cross-clamp** and **cardioplegia** (cold or warm blood, antegrade or retrograde) to arrest the heart.
- **4.** **Distal anastomoses** (vein, radial), then LIMA to LAD, and removal of the cross-clamp; **proximal anastomoses** with a partial clamp or aortic no-touch techniques.
- **5.** **Rewarming**, de-airing, **weaning from CPB**, protamine, haemostasis (Papworth checklist), pacing wires, drains, sternal closure.

Off-pump CABG avoids CPB but still may involve aortic side-clamping for proximal grafts; a true anaortic/no-touch technique specifically minimises aortic manipulation. Heart displacement may sharply reduce output, requiring communication, preload/vasopressor adjustment and readiness to institute CPB.

**Monitoring:** ECG with ST analysis, arterial line before induction, CVC (± PAC), TOE, NIRS, temperature, urine output, ACT.

**Induction and maintenance:** haemodynamic stability and avoiding tachycardia and hypotension (etomidate or propofol titrated, opioid, rocuronium); volatile or TIVA; manage the sternotomy and sternal spread response; antifibrinolytic (TXA), antibiotic prophylaxis, **heparin**.

**Goals:** maintain coronary perfusion (MAP above 65), heart rate 60 to 80, avoid/treat ischaemia (e.g. GTN for spasm if perfusion pressure permits), myocardial protection, temperature control.

**On CPB:** maintain anaesthesia (volatile in the oxygenator or TIVA), MAP 60 to 80, haemodilution, glucose and gas control.

## Postop

After successful separation, give titrated protamine slowly, confirm haemostasis/drain function and transfer with a structured handover. Monitor ischaemia, LV/RV function, rhythm/pacing, bleeding, ventilation, glucose and organ perfusion. Provide multimodal analgesia and assess readiness for early extubation/mobilisation; resume indicated aspirin and secondary prevention when safe.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes sternotomy, conduit harvest, heparin, cannulation and CPB
- Describes cardioplegia and cross-clamp, anastomoses and weaning
- Mentions off-pump alternative
- Preoperative review and drug management
- Monitoring including TOE and arterial line
- Induction and maintenance aims (avoid tachycardia and hypotension)
- Management during CPB and transfer to ICU

items.title: 12. Surgical AVR versus TAVI for aortic stenosis
items.q: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and transcatheter aortic valve implantation, and outline the anaesthetic considerations for severe aortic stenosis in each.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/) · [2024 EACTS perioperative medication guideline](https://academic.oup.com/ejcts/article/67/1/ezae355/7815986)

## Choice of procedure

Use a **Heart Team and lifetime-management decision**, considering frailty, life expectancy, anatomy/access, valve durability, coronary access, concomitant CAD/aortic disease and preferences. Under **2025 ESC/EACTS** guidance, TAVI is recommended for suitable **tricuspid AS at age ≥70**, and SAVR for **<70 with low surgical risk**; remaining patients require individual assessment. These are European recommendations, not a rigid global age rule. Bicuspid/root disease or concomitant CABG/other surgery often favours SAVR. TAVI is no longer confined to high/intermediate surgical risk.

## Physiology and goals in severe aortic stenosis

A fixed outflow obstruction with a hypertrophied, poorly compliant LV: cardiac output and **coronary perfusion** depend on preserved afterload (SVR), sinus rhythm and preload. **Avoid** hypotension, tachycardia, bradycardia and loss of sinus rhythm; maintain preload; use phenylephrine or noradrenaline for hypotension. Unstable AF/tachyarrhythmia warrants prompt synchronised cardioversion; stable AF requires individual rate/rhythm management, treatment of causes and thromboembolic assessment.

## Preop

Confirm AS severity/symptoms, LV/RV function, CAD, access/anatomy and frailty; plan anticoagulation/antiplatelets, rescue and postoperative level of care.

## Intraop

## Surgical AVR

Standard cardiac anaesthesia: arterial line, CVC, TOE (valve, LV, paravalvular leak, de-airing), induction with minimal haemodynamic change, CPB, cardioplegia, rhythm: heart block after replacement needs epicardial pacing; LVOT problems and post-bypass LV hypertrophy cause **dynamic outflow obstruction** (avoid inotropes and hypovolaemia).

## TAVI

- **Location** in a hybrid theatre with surgical and perfusion back-up, **local anaesthetic with sedation or GA** (TOE with GA). The balance is monitoring and avoiding cardiovascular depression.
- **Rapid pacing** may be needed for balloon valvuloplasty/deployment, depending on valve type and technique; rate/duration are operator-specific (often 160–200/min). Confirm pacing capture before deployment and be ready for hypotension, coronary obstruction, tamponade or acute AR rather than assuming every TAVI uses the same pacing sequence.
- **Complications:** vascular injury, annular rupture, coronary obstruction, aortic dissection, stroke, **new conduction block** (permanent pacemaker), paravalvular leak and tamponade; plan for conversion to open surgery.

## Postop

After SAVR monitor bleeding, ventricular function, prosthetic performance, ischaemia and epicardial pacing needs. After TAVI monitor access-site/retroperitoneal bleeding, neurological state, renal function, residual leak and new/delayed AV block; conduction findings determine telemetry, pacing and discharge plan. Prescribe antithrombotics according to current valve guidance and other indications; routine DAPT is not required for every uncomplicated TAVI.

## Self-marking checklist

- Compares surgical AVR and TAVI selection
- Describes aortic stenosis physiology (afterload, rhythm, preload)
- Avoids hypotension and tachycardia; chooses vasopressor
- Surgical AVR anaesthetic points (TOE, pacing, outflow obstruction)
- TAVI: hybrid theatre, pacing, back-up and anaesthetic choice
- Lists TAVI complications and plans
- Follow-up of conduction disturbance

items.title: 13. Anaesthetic issues on bypass and aortic cannulation
items.q: Outline the anaesthetic issues during cardiopulmonary bypass, including the implications of aortic disease for aortic cannulation.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [BJA Education: Anticoagulation for CPB, part one (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9947996/)

## Circuit and conduct

Venous cannulae drain to a reservoir, roller/centrifugal pump, membrane oxygenator/heat exchanger, arterial filter and return cannula. Initial adult flow is often around 2.2–2.4 L/min/m², but adjust to temperature, metabolic demand, DO2, venous saturation and lactate. Individualise MAP (often a 50–80 mmHg CPB range) to perfusion and cerebrovascular disease. Use goal-directed oxygen delivery (normothermic lower threshold around 280–300 mL/min/m²), an agreed temperature plan and usually alpha-stat blood-gas management in adults.

## Anticoagulation

**Heparin:** an initial 300–400 IU/kg is common; verify adequate whole-blood anticoagulation **before CPB and regularly during it**. ACT >480 s is a common target but depends on activator/device/circuit protocol (some validated systems use different thresholds); heparin-concentration monitoring can supplement ACT. Investigate an inadequate response rather than proceeding unprotected. **Protamine is given after successful separation**, titrated to residual heparin where possible, avoiding automatic reversal of the total heparin administered. Contemporary CPB guidance favours a protamine:heparin ratio below 1 mg/100 IU when appropriate, using local monitoring and excluding other causes of prolonged ACT/bleeding. Administer slowly with monitoring for hypotension, PH/RV failure and anaphylaxis.

## Anaesthesia during CPB

Maintain anaesthesia (volatile through the oxygenator or propofol infusion, muscle relaxation), monitor pressure, temperature, urine output, ACT, blood gases, K, glucose, Hb, venous saturation and NIRS; avoid awareness and hypoxia; drug redosing; use the agreed CPB ventilation strategy (cessation, CPAP or low-volume ventilation according to procedure/protocol); fluid balance and haemodilution (avoid a fixed Hct target in isolation: ensure adequate oxygen delivery).

## Aortic cannulation and aortic disease

An atheromatous, calcified or aneurysmal ascending aorta raises the risk of **embolic stroke** during cannulation, clamping and decannulation, and of **dissection**. Preoperative CT, **epiaortic ultrasound** for the cannulation/clamp site and TOE for accessible aortic segments (TOE has a distal ascending-aortic blind spot) guide strategy: move the cannulation site (axillary, femoral or innominate artery), **no-touch** or off-pump techniques, single-clamp or fibrillatory arrest, or circulatory arrest. Monitor for dissection (sudden pressure change, high line pressure, TOE).

## Myocardial protection

Cardioplegia (cold or warm blood or crystalloid; del Nido), antegrade and retrograde, with a cross-clamp, temperature management and monitoring of ECG for electromechanical activity; avoid ventricular distension.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the circuit and flow, pressure and temperature targets
- Heparin dose and ACT; heparin resistance and HIT
- Protamine reversal and its hazards
- Maintains anaesthesia and monitors during CPB
- Aortic disease and the risk of embolism or dissection
- Alternative cannulation and epiaortic or TOE assessment
- Myocardial protection with cardioplegia

items.title: 14. Therapeutic hypothermia: cooling and rewarming problems
items.q: Discuss the physiological effects of therapeutic hypothermia in cardiac surgery and the problems of cooling and rewarming.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Consensus on hypothermia in aortic arch surgery (temperature definitions)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3741830/)

## Why cool

Metabolic rate falls by about 6 to 8% per degree Celsius (Q10 about 2), so **oxygen demand** of brain, heart and viscera falls, allowing lower pump flows and, at 18 to 20 °C, circulatory arrest. For **aortic-arch hypothermic circulatory arrest**, commonly used consensus bands are profound ≤14 °C, deep 14.1–20 °C, moderate 20.1–28 °C and mild 28.1–34 °C. Other contexts use different classifications: state the context and measured temperature. Cooling does not create a guaranteed safe arrest interval.

## Effects by system

| System | Effect |
|---|---|
| **CNS** | Reduced cerebral metabolic rate and blood flow (autoregulation preserved with alpha-stat); EEG slowing; electrocerebral silence occurs at a variable temperature and cannot be inferred from temperature or NIRS alone; amnesia and reduced MAC |
| **Cardiac** | Bradycardia, conduction slowing (J waves), increasing ventricular arrhythmia susceptibility with deeper cooling (no absolute VF threshold); reduced contractility at deep levels but improved myocardial protection |
| **Blood** | Increased viscosity, **platelet dysfunction and sequestration**, impaired coagulation enzymes, fibrinolysis; left shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin curve (reduced tissue offloading) |
| **Acid-base and gases** | Increased gas solubility; pH rises as CO2 solubility rises (alpha-stat versus pH-stat) |
| **Renal and metabolic** | Cold diuresis, hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance, reduced drug clearance |
| **Immune** | Impaired immunity and wound infection |

## Problems at rewarming

- **Rewarm slowly** (arterial outflow temperature at most 37 °C, with monitored oxygenator arterial–venous blood gradients within the perfusion protocol (commonly ≤10 °C, tighter during late rewarming)) to avoid **cerebral hyperthermia**, gas emboli (bubbles come out of solution) and vasodilation.
- **After-drop** (continued core cooling after bypass), shivering (raises oxygen consumption; use warming and titrated anti-shivering treatment accounting for sedation/renal effects), vasoconstriction followed by vasodilatation and hypotension, hypovolaemia, and coagulopathy.
- Management: keep the nasopharyngeal temperature at 36 to 37 °C before separation, forced-air warming, warmed fluids and ventilator humidification, and avoid hyperthermia above 37.5 °C afterwards.

## Self-marking checklist

- Gives the reduction in metabolic rate with cooling and temperature grades
- Describes CNS, cardiac, coagulation and metabolic effects
- Explains the oxygen–haemoglobin shift and gas solubility
- Describes rewarming rate and cerebral hyperthermia risk
- Mentions after-drop and shivering
- Gives practical warming and temperature targets

items.title: 15. Ventricular fibrillation in ICU after cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient fibrillates in the ICU four hours after cardiac surgery. Describe the management, including the role of internal defibrillation.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [ANZCOR 11.10: cardiac surgery/CALS-ANZ (current 2026 page)](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-10-resuscitation-in-special-circumstances) · [ANZSCTS/ANZICS CALS-ANZ primary consensus (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10692601/)

## Differences from a standard arrest

Cardiac arrest after cardiac surgery is most commonly **VF/VT**, tamponade, bleeding, tension pneumothorax, hypoxia or a pacing failure, and the sternum is freshly closed. The compressions can damage grafts or the sternum, and **early resternotomy** is a treatment.

## Management (CALS protocol)

- **1.** **Confirm arrest** (arterial line loss of pulsatility, loss of cardiac output); call the arrest team and **cardiac surgeon**.
- **2.** **Witnessed monitored VF/pulseless VT with an immediately available defibrillator:** deliver up to three rapid stacked biphasic shocks at the recommended device energy, aiming for the initial treatment sequence within one minute. If shocks cannot be delivered immediately, or fail to restore circulation, **start CPR without further delay** while preparing resternotomy. This exception must not cause a prolonged no-flow period.
- **3.** **Do not give adrenaline** (1 mg boluses) routinely: it may cause rebound hypertension and graft disruption; amiodarone 300 mg after three failed shocks.
- **4.** **Pacing:** for asystole/extreme bradycardia, first exclude VF hidden by pacing artefact (briefly pause pacing under expert control if needed); use epicardial pacing at approximately 90/min and high output, confirming mechanical capture. If ineffective, commence CPR and use backup pacing while preparing resternotomy.
- **5.** **Emergency resternotomy within 5 minutes** of the arrest if unresponsive: relieves tamponade, allows direct massage and **internal defibrillation**.
- **6.** Address **reversible causes** (4Hs and 4Ts): tamponade, hypovolaemia, tension pneumothorax, hypoxia, electrolytes, hypothermia.

## Internal defibrillation

Sterile internal paddles applied directly to the heart (anterior and posterior ventricular surfaces), delivering **10 to 20 J** biphasic (lower energy than external because the current passes directly through the myocardium); used with an open chest. Use an internal-paddle energy setting because chest-wall impedance is bypassed; hands must not touch the heart or the paddles; clear the field. Do not delay indicated external/internal defibrillation to deactivate an ICD. Clear all personnel and use device-recommended internal energy; ensure a controlled oxygen/fire-risk environment.

After return of circulation: ECG, echo, electrolytes, ischaemia assessment and ICU.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises arrest causes specific to cardiac surgery
- Gives up to three shocks first, then CPR and resternotomy
- Notes adrenaline and amiodarone modifications
- Pacing for asystole or bradycardia with wires
- Emergency resternotomy within 5 minutes
- Describes internal paddle technique and energy (10 to 20 J)
- Treats reversible causes

items.title: 16. Complications of interventional cardiology procedures
items.q: Outline the major complications of interventional cardiology procedures (including percutaneous coronary intervention and transcatheter valve procedures), their presentation and their management in the catheter laboratory.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: Management of cardiogenic shock after ACS (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140595/) · [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/) · [Blue Book 2021: RV dysfunction pp115–124; VAD noncardiac surgery pp125–134; AF ablation chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book_2021-Version8.pdf?language=en)

## General principles

The cath lab is a remote site: the anaesthetist is called for sedation, a failed procedure or a crisis. Know the complication, call for help early, and anticipate heparin and dual antiplatelet therapy.

| Complication | Presentation | Management |
|---|---|---|
| **Coronary perforation** | Contrast extravasation, hypotension, tamponade | Alert interventionalist/surgeon, balloon occlusion to seal perforation, covered stent/embolisation as appropriate; urgent echo and drainage for tamponade. Decide heparin reversal jointly, balancing ongoing bleeding against fresh-stent/catheter thrombosis; surgery if uncontrolled |
| **Tamponade** (perforation, lead, ablation, TAVI) | Falling blood pressure, rising CVP, echo | Urgent pericardiocentesis/drainage while arranging definitive repair; surgical exploration if perforation/rupture or drainage is inadequate. Resternotomy applies to a previously opened sternum, not every cath-lab tamponade |
| **Acute vessel closure, no-reflow, infarction** | Chest pain, ST change, arrhythmia, shock | Urgent angiographic/operator treatment of closure; treat spasm or microvascular no-reflow with appropriate intracoronary agents under protocol, support perfusion and select MCS if refractory |
| **Arrhythmia and heart block** | VF/VT, bradycardia, block after TAVI or ablation | Defibrillate, pacing wire, drugs |
| **Access-site bleeding and retroperitoneal haematoma** | Hypotension, flank pain, falling Hb | Pressure, ultrasound/CT, transfusion, vascular repair |
| **Stroke or embolism** (air, thrombus, calcium) | New neurology | Stroke call, CT, thrombectomy (consider) |
| **Contrast reaction and contrast nephropathy** | Anaphylaxis; AKI at 24 to 72 hours | Adrenaline; hydration, minimise contrast |
| **Valve complications** (TAVI): annular rupture, coronary obstruction, aortic dissection, valve embolisation, paravalvular leak | Collapse, ischaemia | Surgical back-up, balloon, conversion to open surgery |
| **Radiation, cardiogenic shock, vascular injury** | | Protection; MCS |

## Anaesthetic role

Pre-procedure risk assessment (Heart Team), airway plan, pads on, drugs (vasopressor, inotropes), a surgical team and perfusionist for high-risk cases, and post-procedure monitoring.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies coronary perforation and tamponade with management
- Lists arrhythmia and block, vessel closure and no-reflow
- Access site and retroperitoneal bleeding
- Stroke, contrast reactions and AKI
- Valve procedure complications and surgical back-up
- Anaesthetic role and preparation in a remote site

items.title: 17. Bypass and ECMO support for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the indications for cardiopulmonary bypass and ECMO in non-cardiac surgery and the anaesthetic issues of managing a patient on extracorporeal support.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: The role of ECMO support in airway procedures (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10300492/) · [Blue Book 2017: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: anaesthetic perspectives](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/0cbf08ef-6e16-4b2e-a95f-7713f734d6cb/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book-2017.pdf?language=en) · [ELSO adult VV-ECMO guideline (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8315725/)

## Indications

- **CPB:** resection of tumours with caval or atrial extension (renal cell, hepatic, adrenal), complex aortic or thoracic aneurysm surgery, **rewarming** after severe hypothermia, pulmonary thromboendarterectomy and massive pulmonary embolism.
- **ECMO** (VV or VA): airway surgery with a critical obstruction (tracheal tumour, carinal resection, foreign body) in a patient who cannot be oxygenated or ventilated, **lung transplantation**, thoracic and mediastinal masses with airway or vascular compression, massive pulmonary embolism with arrest, refractory cardiac arrest (E-CPR), and cardiogenic shock.
- Distinguish **elective pre-induction ECMO** (cannulated and flowing), **standby** with a rehearsed access/cannulation plan, and rescue. In critical fixed airway obstruction, rescue after collapse may be too slow: pre-induction cannulation under local anaesthesia may be needed. Merely having an ECMO machine nearby does not ensure oxygenation.

## Configurations

**VV ECMO** supports gas exchange (drains the IVC, returns to the right atrium); **VA ECMO** supports circulation and oxygenation (venous drainage, arterial return, peripheral femoral or central), with a distal limb perfusion cannula.

## Preop

Review CT, graft anatomy, prior operation/anaesthetic record, ventricular/valve function, anticoagulants, organ reserve and available vascular access. Agree re-entry, cannulation and massive-haemorrhage plans with the senior team.

## Intraop

- **Planning:** a multidisciplinary team (surgeon, perfusion, ICU); decide whether to cannulate before induction (local anaesthetic) or standby.
- **Anticoagulation:** heparin (centre-specific anti-Xa/aPTT/ACT targets on ECMO; CPB requires substantially greater anticoagulation) increases surgical bleeding; manage with cell salvage and monitoring (TEG), individualised platelet/fibrinogen targets and targeted products; a universal platelet target >100 ×10⁹/L is not required for every nonbleeding ECMO patient.
- **Monitoring:** arterial line (right radial in peripheral VA ECMO: differential hypoxia, the harlequin syndrome), pre- and post-oxygenator saturations, NIRS, flow, and temperature.
- **Anaesthesia:** TIVA is often practical, particularly with absent lung ventilation; circuit sequestration and altered pharmacokinetics can change dose requirements. Approved CPB oxygenators can deliver volatile anaesthetic via a calibrated vaporiser, gas monitoring and scavenging; do not assume every ECMO oxygenator is approved/effective for this. Confirm the actual delivery route. Processed EEG is an adjunct and cannot guarantee adequate delivery/absence of awareness. Agree lung-rest versus operative apnoea and monitor haemodynamics.
- **Complications:** bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis, air embolism, circuit failure, clots, infection, and stroke (intracranial haemorrhage is the most devastating).
- Candidacy: assess reversibility/exit strategy, neurological prognosis, bleeding risk, frailty and comorbidities. Age alone is not a universal absolute contraindication.

## Postop

Transfer with explicit circuit/ventilator settings, anticoagulation targets, cannula checks, analgesia/sedation and bleeding/perfusion plans. Assess neurological/organ recovery, mobilisation and the pathway to weaning or definitive treatment.

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists CPB indications in non-cardiac surgery
- Lists ECMO indications (airway, transplant, PE, cardiac arrest)
- Describes VV versus VA configurations
- Plans team, cannulation timing and anticoagulation
- Monitoring including differential hypoxia and pre- and post-oxygenator saturations
- TIVA and depth of anaesthesia
- Complications and contraindications

items.title: 18. Neurological complications of cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the neurological complications of cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass and the strategies to reduce them.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [ERAS Cardiac/ERAS/STS joint consensus, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38284956/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/)

## Complications

- **Stroke** (1 to 3% in CABG, higher with valve and aortic surgery) and **TIA**; mortality is high.
- **Postoperative delirium** and delayed neurocognitive recovery/postoperative neurocognitive disorder. Rates vary widely by test, age, baseline function, procedure and follow-up; avoid unqualified “up to 50%” figures. Delirium is an acute fluctuating disturbance of attention/awareness, not synonymous with long-term cognitive decline.
- Encephalopathy, seizures, peripheral nerve injury (brachial plexus, ulnar), retinal and visual loss, and spinal cord injury in aortic surgery.

## Mechanisms

**Embolic** (atheromatous aortic debris from cannulation and clamping, air, particulate and fat, thrombus from AF or the left ventricle, valve calcium), **hypoperfusion** (low MAP on CPB, particularly with carotid or intracranial stenosis and impaired autoregulation), **inflammation** and blood–brain barrier disruption, haemodilution, hyperthermia on rewarming, hyperglycaemia and microemboli.

## Risk factors

Age, prior stroke or carotid disease, aortic atheroma, AF, diabetes, long CPB time, valve and aortic surgery, endocarditis, and low EF.

## Strategies

## Preop

Baseline cognition/neurology and risk assessment; carotid imaging/CT of the aorta when indicated rather than routine testing of everyone; optimise AF, perfusion and metabolic status. Discuss risks.

## Intraop

- **Aortic manipulation:** epiaortic ultrasound, no-touch techniques, alternative cannulation, single clamp.
- **During CPB:** MAP 65 to 80 (higher in cerebrovascular disease), **avoid hyperthermia** (rewarm slowly), moderate protocol-based glucose control while avoiding hypoglycaemia, adequate haemoglobin, **NIRS** monitoring, arterial line filters, CO2 flooding of the field, careful de-airing, and avoid venous obstruction.
- **Anaesthetic:** appropriate depth/EEG assessment (processed indices are adjuncts, not guarantees), minimise unnecessary benzodiazepines/anticholinergics, adequate analgesia and temperature control. NIRS desaturation should trigger systematic assessment, but routine NIRS has not established a universal reduction in stroke/cognitive injury.

## Postop

Screen for delirium (e.g. CAM-ICU), assess new focal deficits early, protect sleep, enable glasses/hearing aids and orientation, mobilise and treat pain; correct hypoxia, metabolic abnormalities and drug causes.

- **If stroke occurs:** urgent CT/angiography, thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion in selected cases, blood pressure and glucose control, and rehabilitation.

## Self-marking checklist

- Distinguishes stroke, delirium and perioperative neurocognitive disorders without unqualified incidence claims
- Embolic, hypoperfusion and inflammatory mechanisms
- Risk factors
- Aortic no-touch and epiaortic strategies
- CPB strategies: MAP, temperature, glucose, NIRS
- Delirium prevention
- Management of established stroke

items.title: 19. ECMO for severe respiratory failure
items.q: Outline the indications for ECMO in severe respiratory failure and the principles of its delivery.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: VV ECMO in severe acute respiratory failure (2024), indexed record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38481419/) · [ELSO adult VV-ECMO guideline (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8315725/) · [EOLIA primary RCT, NEJM 2018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29791822/) · [CESAR primary RCT, Lancet 2009](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19762075/)

## Indications

Consider **VV ECMO** for severe, potentially reversible respiratory failure despite optimised lung-protective care, including prone positioning when appropriate: **PaO2/FiO2 <80 mmHg**, or severe hypercapnia with **pH <7.25 and PaCO2 ≥60 mmHg** despite safe ventilator optimisation (ELSO 2021). Contact an ECMO centre early rather than waiting for irreversible injury; these thresholds prompt expert assessment, not automatic cannulation.

The EOLIA trial used persistent thresholds such as P/F <50 for >3 h, <80 for >6 h, or severe respiratory acidosis for >6 h despite optimised ventilation. Other indications include severe asthma, selected graft failure/pulmonary haemorrhage and bridge to lung transplantation. **Do not infer a fixed 50%/80% mortality from P/F 150/100.**

**Evidence:** EOLIA (2018) found 60-day mortality 35% with early ECMO versus 46% with conventional care/rescue ECMO (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.55–1.04; P=0.09); the primary comparison was not statistically significant and crossover complicates interpretation. CESAR (2009) tested referral to an ECMO centre versus conventional care, not ECMO versus identical expert care for every patient. Together with subsequent evidence and guideline synthesis, these support carefully selected centre-based use; neither is a universal survival guarantee.

**Candidacy/limitations:** the key absolute limitation is anticipated nonrecovery without a viable decannulation/transplant plan. Irreversible neurological injury, major uncontrolled bleeding, immunosuppression, frailty/advanced age and prolonged injurious ventilation are important relative considerations; avoid a rigid age-75 cutoff or treating every anticoagulation concern as absolute.

## Principles of delivery

- **Circuit/cannulation:** venous drainage, centrifugal pump, membrane lung/heat exchanger and venous return. Common arrangements are femoral drainage–jugular return or a dual-lumen jugular cannula under imaging. Position and separation of drainage/return streams limit recirculation. VV ECMO does not directly support systemic circulation.
- **Gas exchange:** systemic oxygenation depends on effective ECMO blood flow relative to cardiac output, Hb, oxygenator performance, recirculation and native lung function. CO2 removal is mainly adjusted by sweep gas. Avoid abrupt PaCO2 correction, especially with chronic hypercapnia. ECCO2R is a distinct lower-flow strategy and does not provide equivalent oxygenation support.
- **Anticoagulation:** commonly UFH, using the centre’s anti-Xa/aPTT/ACT and bleeding/thrombosis protocol. Selected bleeding patients may temporarily need reduced/no anticoagulation with expert monitoring. Platelet/fibrinogen targets depend on bleeding and procedures; >100 ×10⁹/L platelets is not universal.
- **Lung protection:** low plateau/driving pressures and tidal volumes, adequate PEEP and individual oxygenation goals; avoid worsening ventilator injury while extracorporeal support permits recovery. Support nutrition, mobilisation where feasible and organ perfusion.
- **Complications:** bleeding/ICH, thrombosis, haemolysis, infection, cannula malposition/recirculation, air/circuit failure and vascular injury. Arterial limb ischaemia is especially a peripheral **VA** complication; it is not the defining VV cannulation risk.
- **Weaning:** assess lung recovery, reduce sweep/oxygenator gas support and perform monitored off-sweep testing while maintaining safe circuit blood flow to avoid thrombosis. Do not routinely reduce VV blood flow towards zero as a weaning trial. Decannulate after sustained adequate gas exchange and acceptable work of breathing.
- **Transport/procedures:** plan an experienced retrieval team and contingency for deterioration; some patients travel on ECMO, while others can be transferred before cannulation. Ensure anaesthesia delivery/monitoring and a clear emergency circuit plan for procedures.

## Self-marking checklist

- Uses current ELSO refractory-hypoxaemia/hypercapnia criteria, optimised conventional care and early referral
- Distinguishes CESAR referral strategy from EOLIA and accurately interprets the mortality result
- Lists contraindications
- Describes the circuit and cannulation
- Explains oxygenation versus CO2 clearance
- Anticoagulation and lung-protective ventilation
- Complications and weaning

items.title: 20. IABP with falling augmentation and a cold leg
items.q: A patient with an intra-aortic balloon pump develops a falling augmentation pressure and a cold left leg. Describe how you would troubleshoot the device and its complications.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: Management of cardiogenic shock after ACS (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140595/) · [IABP-SHOCK II primary RCT, NEJM 2012](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1208410)

## Assess the device

The balloon is helium-driven (30 to 50 mL), triggered by the ECG or arterial waveform, inflating in diastole and deflating in systole; the console shows the **arterial waveform with augmentation (augmented diastolic pressure often exceeds native systolic pressure, but this is not guaranteed or the sole measure of benefit)**.

**Timing errors**

| Error | Waveform | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Early inflation | Inflation before the dicrotic notch | Premature aortic valve closure, reduced stroke volume |
| Late inflation | Gap after the notch | Reduced coronary augmentation |
| Early deflation | Premature fall/truncation of diastolic augmentation, sometimes a rebound before systole | Less diastolic coronary support and loss of sustained presystolic unloading; waveform details depend on loading/trigger |
| Late deflation | Assisted end-diastolic pressure may be elevated; sluggish/widened systolic upstroke as ejection meets the balloon | **Increased afterload** and impeded ejection |

**Other causes of poor augmentation:** low volume, **balloon too small or malpositioned**, tachycardia or irregular rhythm (AF or ectopics), low SVR or hypovolaemia, a kinked catheter, a gas leak (loss of helium), and **balloon rupture** (blood in the tubing or alarm).

## Complications

- **Limb ischaemia** (the commonest; cold, pulseless leg) and compartment syndrome: reposition, remove the catheter, vascular review.
- **Bleeding** and haematoma, retroperitoneal haemorrhage, **thrombocytopenia** and haemolysis, aortic dissection or perforation, **stroke or embolism** (left subclavian or visceral malperfusion if too high), infection, and balloon rupture (stop the pump, remove).
- Left arm and renal malperfusion if the balloon is displaced.

## Management and weaning

**Cold leg is an urgent limb-threat problem:** call vascular/cardiac specialists immediately; assess pulses/Doppler, colour, temperature, sensation/movement, catheter side/position and compartment pressure if indicated. Consider removal/repositioning, alternative access or vascular intervention while maintaining alternative haemodynamic support; do not await routine weaning. Check for bleeding/retroperitoneal haematoma and review anticoagulation. For ordinary recovery, reassess perfusion/echo and wean ratio or balloon volume according to the device/centre protocol; complete deflation and expert removal with haemostasis checks. With suspected rupture/blood in gas tubing, stop pumping, disconnect as directed and arrange urgent removal—do not keep reinflating.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes balloon mechanism and waveform
- Identifies timing errors (early and late inflation/deflation) and effects
- Other causes of poor augmentation (rhythm, volume, position, leak)
- Lists complications, especially limb ischaemia
- Actions for balloon rupture
- Describes weaning and removal

items.title: 21. Duration of ventilation and fast-track after cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the factors that influence the duration of postoperative ventilation after cardiac surgery and the role of fast-track management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [ERAS Cardiac/ERAS/STS joint consensus, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38284956/) · [BJA Education: Perioperative care in cardiac surgery (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8446225/)

## Fast-track and enhanced recovery

Fast-track originated in the 1980s to cut ICU cost by **early extubation** (within 6 hours, often in 1 to 4 hours); it is now part of a broader **enhanced recovery** pathway (ERAS Cardiac Society): prehabilitation, patient information, optimised anaemia and glycaemia, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, antifibrinolytics, normothermia, early mobilisation when physiologically ready under the local enhanced-recovery pathway, early nutrition, and delirium screening. Adherence to the pathway improves outcomes.

## Factors influencing duration of ventilation

| Group | Factors |
|---|---|
| **Patient** | Age, frailty, poor LV function, COPD, obesity or OSA, renal impairment, preoperative stroke, anaemia |
| **Surgical** | Emergency, redo or complex surgery, long CPB or cross-clamp time, deep hypothermic arrest, bleeding |
| **Anaesthetic** | High-dose opioid, long-acting drugs, residual neuromuscular block, hypothermia, awareness |
| **Postoperative** | Bleeding or tamponade, haemodynamic instability, low output, vasoplegia, arrhythmia, acute lung injury, atelectasis, pleural effusion, AKI, pain, delirium |

## Preop

Assess frailty, pulmonary/cardiac function, baseline cognition, nutrition and anticipated complexity; agree an individual recovery plan and educate the patient.

## Intraop

- **Anaesthetic for early extubation:** short-acting agents (propofol, remifentanil or low-dose opioids, volatile), regional or local infiltration, avoid hypothermia, minimal neuromuscular block with reversal, with selection based on current stability and recovery criteria; higher preoperative risk alone does not automatically exclude enhanced recovery.

## Postop

- **Criteria** for extubation: warm, haemodynamically stable, bleeding below about 100 mL/h, awake with airway protection, adequate gas exchange/analgesia and quantitative neuromuscular recovery (TOF ratio ≥0.9).
- **Cautions:** do not extubate unstable or bleeding patients just to meet a time target; failure leads to reintubation.

**Routine and emergent ICU management:** monitoring of drains, haemodynamics, ECG and pacing wires, glucose, analgesia, antibiotics and thromboprophylaxis; recognise tamponade, bleeding and arrhythmia early.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines fast-track and enhanced recovery
- Lists patient and surgical factors prolonging ventilation
- Lists anaesthetic and postoperative factors
- Describes anaesthetic technique for early extubation
- Gives extubation criteria
- Cautions on safety versus time targets
- Mentions routine and emergent ICU monitoring

items.title: 22. Failure to reach target ACT and HIT for bypass
items.q: A patient fails to reach an ACT of 480 seconds after 400 units/kg of heparin before cardiopulmonary bypass. Outline your approach, and describe the management of a patient with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia requiring bypass.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: Anticoagulation for CPB, part one (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9947996/) · [BJA Education: Anticoagulation for CPB, part 2 (2023), indexed record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37389280/) · [ASH guideline: HIT, cardiovascular-surgery recommendations 4.1–4.2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6258919/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/)

## Heparin resistance

An inadequate ACT response to a usual heparin dose; definitions vary (often >400–500 IU/kg needed to achieve the locally validated ACT target). Verify the test/dose and anticoagulation adequacy before CPB; a dose threshold alone does not diagnose the cause.

**Causes:** **antithrombin deficiency** (congenital, or acquired with preoperative heparin, liver disease, DIC), increased heparin-binding proteins (including PF4), inflammation and thrombocytosis; raised factor VIII/fibrinogen may alter apparent clotting-test response, thrombocytosis, and drug interactions (andexanet alfa can cause heparin resistance through binding/interference with the heparin-activated antithrombin complex).

**Approach**

- **1.** Confirm vial, dose, IV delivery, sampling and ACT device/activator; repeat if unexpected. Check antithrombin and consider a heparin-concentration or appropriate laboratory anti-Xa assay with specialist interpretation. APTT is not the main monitor for high-dose CPB heparin. Distinguish inadequate drug effect from an assay/acute-phase effect; do not start bypass until the team confirms adequate anticoagulation.
- **2.** Give additional UFH and recheck according to the validated protocol. If antithrombin deficient, give antithrombin concentrate (dose guided by level/product/protocol); plasma is an alternative when appropriate, with a larger volume/transfusion burden. Do not use a fixed dose ceiling or repeated heparin/AT without reassessing the mechanism.
- **3.** Consider alternative anticoagulants (bivalirudin) if still failing.

## Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

- **Immune HIT** is a prothrombotic response to PF4–heparin complexes, typically a >50% platelet fall around days 5–10 after exposure or earlier with recent sensitisation; absolute platelet count may remain normal. A biphasic platelet fall after CPB is more suspicious than an isolated immediate dilutional fall. A mild early nonimmune platelet fall is not the same disease.
- **Diagnosis:** assess 4Ts and timing, send PF4 immunoassay and a functional assay as indicated. Do not diagnose HIT solely from a postoperative positive immunoassay. With intermediate/high suspicion, stop all heparin (including flushes) and start an appropriate nonheparin anticoagulant unless contraindicated; involve haematology. LMWH cross-reacts and is unsuitable for active HIT.
- **Preop:** if surgery can wait, defer until functional testing is negative (subacute HIT B) or antibodies are absent (remote HIT). This is **laboratory phase-based**, not a compulsory 100-day wait.
- **Intraop urgent CPB during acute HIT/subacute HIT A:** bivalirudin is a preferred experienced-centre option; there is no reversal agent. Adjust for renal impairment, use validated dosing/ACT or other monitoring, avoid stagnant blood in closed circuit segments and plan cardiotomy suction/field blood management. Argatroban can be considered with severe renal dysfunction in an expert protocol, but hepatic clearance, prolonged effect and bleeding are major concerns. Plasma exchange plus intraoperative heparin, or heparin with a potent antiplatelet strategy, are specialist alternatives with limited evidence—not routine combinations to improvise.
