- **Subacute HIT B** (platelets recovered, functional assay negative, immunoassay positive) or **remote HIT:** intraoperative heparin confined to CPB may be used under guideline/expert advice; avoid heparin before/after. “Subacute” without A/B distinction is unsafe shorthand.
- **Postop:** use appropriate nonheparin thromboprophylaxis/anticoagulation and monitor platelets and thrombosis/bleeding. Warfarin initiation in acute HIT waits for platelet recovery and requires appropriate overlap with nonheparin anticoagulation.

## Self-marking checklist

- Defines heparin resistance on CPB
- Lists causes (antithrombin deficiency, non-specific binding)
- Distinguishes true from pseudo-resistance
- Treats with extra heparin, antithrombin or plasma
- Distinguishes HIT type 1 and type 2 and the 4T score
- Bivalirudin or argatroban for urgent surgery; LMWH contraindicated
- Uses HIT phase/functional assay rather than a fixed waiting period; distinguishes subacute A from B

items.title: 23. Redo cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the specific anaesthetic and surgical issues associated with redo cardiac surgery.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X) · [ERAS Cardiac/ERAS/STS joint consensus, 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38284956/) · [BJA Education: Perioperative care in cardiac surgery (2021)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8446225/)

## Why it is different

Redo cardiac surgery (repeat sternotomy) now includes valve replacement after CABG, degenerated bioprosthesis, congenital repair and transplant. Patients are older, more comorbid, and have more complex pathology; mortality is higher than for first-time surgery (EuroSCORE).

## Surgical issues

- **Re-entry hazard:** adhesions with the heart, great vessels, a patent **LIMA graft** or the right ventricle lying directly behind the sternum can be torn on sternotomy, causing catastrophic bleeding.
- Preoperative **CT** to define the distance between sternum and heart, graft position and aortic calcification.
- Alternatives: peripheral cannulation (femoral vessels or axillary artery) and **CPB before sternotomy**, a lateral or minithoracotomy, or transcatheter options.
- Longer operations, more bleeding, longer CPB and cross-clamp times, and poorer myocardial protection (non-flowing grafts, retrograde cardioplegia).

## Preop

Review CT, graft anatomy, prior operation/anaesthetic record, ventricular/valve function, anticoagulants, organ reserve and available vascular access. Agree re-entry, cannulation and massive-haemorrhage plans with the senior team.

## Intraop

- **Planning:** a Heart Team discussion; consent for higher risk; senior surgeon and perfusionist.
- **Large-bore access** (two), arterial line, defibrillator pads (external) in place **before sternotomy**, blood/component availability matched to anticipated risk and local massive-haemorrhage logistics, cell salvage, antifibrinolytic (TXA), viscoelastic tests, and a fibrinogen plan.
- Anticipate **massive haemorrhage** at re-entry: ability to go on bypass via femoral cannulation immediately.
- Prior sternotomy and **previous arterial grafts**: protect the LIMA, consider the radial artery side.
- TOE for ventricular/valve assessment and de-airing (it cannot reliably confirm patency of every coronary graft); plan for prolonged CPB (inotropes, vasopressors, RV support).

## Postop

ICU handover should highlight graft/re-entry injuries, myocardial protection and cannulation sites. Monitor bleeding/tamponade, low output/RV dysfunction, vasoplegia, renal/respiratory injury, limb perfusion and neurological state; plan ventilation, analgesia and antithrombotic restart.

## Self-marking checklist

- Describes the re-entry hazard and patent graft risk
- Preoperative CT planning and cannulation alternatives
- Longer CPB, bleeding and poorer protection
- Large-bore access, pads before sternotomy and cell salvage
- Plan for femoral bypass at re-entry
- Blood products, TXA and viscoelastic tests
- ICU and postoperative complications

items.title: 2026.2 Q9: Failure to wean from bypass after CABG
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q9 · no examiner's report yet
items.q: Describe your approach to the management of a patient who has failed to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** Paper verified; no examiner report available in the Learn index at audit. Model/checklist are educational synthesis. [Official source](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/125203). These checklists are not official College marking schedules.

> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Blue Book 2021: RV dysfunction pp115–124; VAD noncardiac surgery pp125–134; AF ablation chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book_2021-Version8.pdf?language=en)

## Principle

A failed wean is a **diagnostic problem under time pressure**. Maintain or promptly restore adequate bypass flow and systemic perfusion, avoid ventricular distension with appropriate venting, and work through a structured list rather than escalating inotropes blindly. Communicate with the surgeon and perfusionist throughout.

## 1. Confirm the basics (on bypass)

- **Rate and rhythm:** AV-sequential pacing for heart block with sinus atrial activity; VVI with AF. Synchronised cardioversion for an unstable organised tachyarrhythmia; **unsynchronised defibrillation for VF/pulseless VT**. Individualise rate (often 80–100/min initially) to filling, output and ischaemia.
- **Metabolic:** near-normothermia without cerebral hyperthermia; correct important potassium, ionised calcium, magnesium and acid–base abnormalities, and assess glucose, Hb, blood gases and oxygen delivery. Do not prescribe hyperkalaemia as a universal target.
- **Ventilation:** lungs re-expanded, no pneumothorax or secretions, FiO2 1.0, no hypercarbia.
- **Anaesthesia:** adequate depth; drugs given in the last minutes (protamine not yet).

## 2. Find the cause: TOE, pressures and direct vision

| Cause | Clue | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **LV failure from ischaemia** (graft kink, thrombosis, air in a coronary, poor myocardial protection) | Regional wall motion abnormality, ST change | Surgeon checks grafts (flow measurement), revise or add graft, GTN for spasm |
| **RV failure** (right coronary air/ischaemia, pulmonary hypertension; protamine only if already administered) | Dilated poorly contracting RV, septal shift, high CVP with low output; PA pressure may be high or fall in advanced failure | Correct cause, protect systemic/RV coronary perfusion, optimise filling and ventilation; inhaled pulmonary vasodilator and inotrope |
| **Vasoplegia** | Preserved function, low SVR with normal/high output and hypoperfusion | Noradrenaline with early vasopressin; refractory cases may need methylene blue after checking serotonergic drugs/G6PD deficiency and other contraindications |
| **Hypovolaemia or bleeding** | Underfilled LV; interpret with RV size, bleeding and venous drainage | Carefully restore filling from circuit/fluids/blood, reassess TOE and surgical bleeding |
| **Mechanical obstruction/structural problem** | TOE and direct inspection: valve dysfunction, dynamic LVOT obstruction/SAM, graft issue, aortic injury, compressive collection; clinical assessment for tension pneumothorax | Correct the specific lesion with the surgeon; dynamic LVOTO needs filling/afterload support and reduction of inappropriate inotropy |
| **Heart block** | ECG | Epicardial pacing |

## 3. Treat in order

Optimise **preload**, **rate and rhythm**, **contractility** (dobutamine or adrenaline, then milrinone) and **afterload** with a vasopressor to keep the MAP above 65. Use inhaled nitric oxide or iloprost for a high PVR.

## 4. If still failing

- **Reperfusion and reassessment:** maintain/return to adequate CPB support while correcting the cause; allow myocardial recovery and reassess function. Duration is individualised, not a fixed 15–30-minute rule. Avoid repeated traumatic failed attempts.
- **Select support for the failing ventricle:** IABP can assist selected LV ischaemia/low-output states and sometimes RV coronary perfusion, but does not directly replace RV output. Severe isolated RV failure may require RVAD; biventricular/cardiopulmonary failure may require VA-ECMO.
- **Mechanical support:** central or peripheral VA-ECMO, or a ventricular assist device. Leave the chest open if swelling or bleeding prevents closure.

**Postop:** agree the support and ICU plan before leaving theatre: haemodynamics, repeat echo, lactate/organ perfusion, ventilation, bleeding and anticoagulation, and a plan to reassess/wean any MCS. Protamine reversal follows successful separation; if bypass must be restarted after reversal, re-heparinise and confirm anticoagulation.
rubric: Stays on bypass and works through a structured approach
Checks rate and rhythm (pacing, cardioversion), metabolic state, ventilation and anaesthesia
Uses TOE and pressures to find LV, RV, valve, tamponade or vasoplegic causes
Takes graft problems, air and protamine reaction as causes
Gives inotropes, vasopressors and pulmonary vasodilators in a logical sequence
Describes resting the heart on bypass
Escalates to IABP, ECMO or ventricular assist device

items.title: 2019.2 Q1: Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest: rationale and consequences
items.q: Describe the rationale for the use of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest and outline the pathophysiological consequences of this technique.
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** Report emphasis: cerebral protection and consequences including coagulopathy, arrhythmia and neurological injury; do not confuse DHCA with cardioplegia, CPB or ECMO. [Official source](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106437). These checklists are not official College marking schedules.

> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Consensus on hypothermia in aortic arch surgery (temperature definitions)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3741830/)

## Rationale

**Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA)** stops the circulation completely, at a core temperature of about 18 to 20 °C, so the surgeon has a **bloodless, cannula-free field** (aortic arch surgery, type A dissection, some thoracoabdominal and congenital procedures, pulmonary thromboendarterectomy). The risk is organ ischaemia, and the aim is **cerebral protection**.

Cooling markedly reduces cerebral oxygen consumption (often described as roughly 6–7% per °C over part of the clinical range), but does not abolish metabolism or ischaemic injury. There is **no guaranteed safe arrest time**: risk rises with duration and depends on actual brain temperature, embolic load and cerebral perfusion. Approximately 30 minutes is a historical planning reference for isolated DHCA, not a safety guarantee.

## Technique

- Cool with CPB using monitored arterial outlet/venous blood and patient temperatures, respecting heat-exchanger gradients and avoiding gaseous emboli. Nasopharyngeal plus a slower core site assess temperature distribution; EEG can assess electrocerebral activity when available. **NIRS measures regional oxygenation and cannot confirm EEG silence or adequate global brain cooling.**
- Cerebral protection: minimise arrest duration, meticulous de-airing/embolism prevention and an agreed selective antegrade cerebral perfusion strategy where appropriate (often permitting warmer arrest); retrograde perfusion is used in selected protocols. Topical head cooling is an adjunct. Routine steroids/barbiturates have no established outcome benefit as neuroprotection; avoid hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia.
- Rewarm slowly (avoid cerebral hyperthermia, outflow temperature below 37 °C) to prevent gas emboli and brain injury.

## Pathophysiological consequences

| System | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Neurological** | Stroke, delirium, seizures, cognitive deficit, choreoathetosis in children; risk rises with arrest time |
| **Coagulation** | Platelet dysfunction, slowed enzyme activity, fibrinolysis, heparin and haemodilution: major bleeding |
| **Cardiac** | Bradycardia, VF below about 28 °C, arrhythmias on rewarming, myocardial stunning |
| **Respiratory** | Left shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin curve, altered solubility of gases (pH-stat or alpha-stat strategy), lung injury |
| **Renal and visceral** | Ischaemia–reperfusion injury, acute kidney injury, gut ischaemia, cold diuresis |
| **Metabolic** | Hyperglycaemia (insulin resistance), acidosis, electrolyte shifts, systemic inflammatory response |

Postoperative: prolonged ventilation, delayed awakening, bleeding and tamponade.
rubric: Defines DHCA (temperature about 18 to 20 °C, complete circulatory arrest)
Gives the rationale: bloodless field with cerebral protection
Explains the fall in cerebral metabolic rate with cooling
Explains duration-dependent risk without claiming a safe time; distinguishes cerebral perfusion, EEG and NIRS
Lists neurological consequences
Lists coagulopathy and arrhythmias
Mentions renal, metabolic and rewarming problems
Does not confuse DHCA with cardioplegia or ECMO

items.title: 2016.2 Q10: Considerations for successful weaning from bypass after CABG
items.q: Outline the considerations for successful weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass after coronary artery graft surgery.
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** Report minimum: native circulation, native ventilation and metabolic/haematological correction. [Official source](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106431). These checklists are not official College marking schedules.

> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Blue Book 2021: RV dysfunction pp115–124; VAD noncardiac surgery pp125–134; AF ablation chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book_2021-Version8.pdf?language=en) · [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X)

## Principle

Weaning is the **return of the native circulation and ventilation** once the heart and the patient are ready. Prepare before the surgeon removes the clamp and complete a checklist.

## 1. Native circulation

- **Rate and rhythm:** sinus 80 to 100 per minute (or paced), no block or ectopy; defibrillate or cardiovert if needed.
- **Volume and MAP:** adequate preload (TOE and CVP), MAP above 65 mmHg with vasopressor if needed.
- **Contractility and ischaemia:** good function on TOE, no new regional wall motion abnormality or ST change, graft flows checked.
- **De-airing** of the heart, vents off, cross-clamp off.

## 2. Native ventilation

Lungs **re-expanded** under vision (recruitment, check for pneumothorax or secretions), FiO2 1.0, and a working circuit before ventilation restarts.

## 3. Metabolic and haematological

- **Temperature** above 36 °C (nasopharyngeal) and a small core–periphery gradient.
- **Acid-base and gases:** correct significant disturbances; potassium in an appropriate normal range and adequate ionised calcium/magnesium. Treat hyperkalaemia as well as hypokalaemia; no universal K 4.5–5.5 target.
- **Haemoglobin/oxygen delivery:** assess Hb with cardiac output, SvO2, lactate, bleeding and ischaemia. A restrictive transfusion threshold around 75 g/L can suit stable cardiac-surgery patients, but is not a universal weaning prerequisite or appropriate for every actively ischaemic/bleeding patient; control glucose without hypoglycaemia.
- **Coagulation:** assess anticipated bleeding and have products/testing ready. **Remain adequately heparinised for separation; protamine is given only after successful separation and agreement that immediate CPB is unlikely.** Afterwards assess residual heparin, bleeding, platelets/fibrinogen and surgical haemostasis (Papworth checklist). Stop cardiotomy suction at protamine administration according to the perfusion protocol.

## 4. Anaesthesia and equipment

Adequate depth and analgesia; transducers zeroed, TOE ready, **epicardial pacing wires tested**, defibrillator pads, and inotropes, vasopressors, vasodilators (GTN, nitric oxide) drawn up.

## 5. The process

Communicate with surgeon/perfusionist; restore ventilation and gradually transfer filling/workload to the heart as the perfusionist reduces bypass support under direct vision, pressure monitoring and TOE. Avoid abrupt filling or ventricular distension; review repair/grafts, LV/RV function and de-airing. If unstable, restore adequate CPB promptly, diagnose and correct the cause, then consider appropriately selected MCS. After stable separation, reverse heparin carefully and reassess haemostasis and perfusion.
rubric: Native circulation: rate, rhythm, volume, MAP and contractility
Checks de-airing and graft flows
Native ventilation: lungs re-expanded with FiO2 1.0
Metabolic: temperature, acid-base, electrolytes
Haemoglobin and coagulation (anticoagulation maintained until separation, then protamine/haemostasis)
Anaesthesia, monitoring, pacing wires and drugs ready
Gradual wean with communication and a failure plan

items.title: 2012.2 Q3: Prerequisites for separation and causes of post-bypass hypotension
items.q:
1. What are the prerequisites for separation from standard cardiopulmonary bypass after uneventful coronary artery bypass surgery? (50%)

2. What are the likely causes of hypotension in the immediate post-separation period? (50%)
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** Report emphasis: restoration of native output/ventilation and correction of CPB disturbances; classify hypotension by pump, rhythm, preload and afterload. Preserve 50%/50% balance. [Official source](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106423). These checklists are not official College marking schedules.

> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Blue Book 2021: RV dysfunction pp115–124; VAD noncardiac surgery pp125–134; AF ablation chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book_2021-Version8.pdf?language=en)

## 1. Prerequisites for separation (50%)

**Restoration of the native cardiac output and ventilation**

- Heart: stable **rhythm** (sinus or paced, rate 80 to 100), no ischaemia, good contractility on TOE, de-aired, grafts flowing.
- **Lungs** re-expanded and ventilated with oxygen, no pneumothorax.
- **Volume and pressure:** adequate preload (CVP, TOE) and MAP.

**Correction of the disturbances of surgery and extracorporeal circulation**

- **Temperature** above 36 °C at the nasopharynx.
- **Acid-base and gas exchange:** pH, PaO2, PaCO2; correct potassium abnormalities and ensure adequate ionised calcium and magnesium.
- **Anaemia/haemostasis:** ensure sufficient oxygen delivery using Hb, flow, SvO2, lactate and clinical context, and assess coagulation disturbance. Continue CPB-level anticoagulation through separation; **protamine/ACT reassessment follow successful separation**, with products guided by bleeding, labs and viscoelastic testing.

**Anaesthetic and equipment**

- Adequate **anaesthesia and analgesia**; ventilator, monitors zeroed, TOE, pacing wires, defibrillator, and inotropes and vasopressors prepared.

## 2. Causes of hypotension after separation (50%)

| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Pump failure** (primary or secondary) | LV stunning, ischaemia from graft problems or air, **RV failure** (air in the right coronary artery, pulmonary hypertension), valve dysfunction |
| **Rate and rhythm** | Bradycardia, heart block, AF, ventricular arrhythmia |
| **Preload** | Hypovolaemia, bleeding, pooling from vasodilators, **tamponade**, tension pneumothorax, high PEEP |
| **Afterload** | **Vasoplegia** (systemic inflammatory response, drugs, ACE inhibitors), **protamine reaction**, anaphylaxis, sepsis, vasodilator infusions |
| **Other** | Residual anaesthetic, acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia |

**Approach:** TOE and the PA catheter to separate causes, treat the cause, and communicate with the surgeon.
rubric: Native circulation: rhythm, rate, volume, MAP and contractility
Lungs re-expanded and ventilating
Temperature, acid-base, electrolytes
Anaemia and coagulation corrected
Adequate anaesthesia and equipment prepared
Hypotension: pump failure (LV and RV), rate and rhythm, preload, afterload
Includes protamine reaction, tamponade and vasoplegia

items.title: 2008.2 Q12: Intra-aortic balloon pump: indications, contraindications and optimisation
items.q: List the indications and contra-indications for the use of an intra-aortic balloon pump. Describe how its performance is optimised.
items.model:
> **Examiner alignment:** Report allocation: indications 3 marks, contraindications 2, optimisation 3, global 2; detailed balloon timing differentiates good answers. Current trial evidence qualifies historical broad indications. [Official source](https://learn.anzca.edu.au/d2l/le/lessons/7841/topics/106406). These checklists are not official College marking schedules.

> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: Management of cardiogenic shock after ACS (2023)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10140595/) · [IABP-SHOCK II primary RCT, NEJM 2012](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1208410)

## Principle

A 30 to 50 mL helium-filled balloon in the **descending thoracic aorta**, **inflated in diastole and deflated just before systole**. Diastolic augmentation raises the aortic diastolic pressure and **coronary perfusion**; systolic deflation reduces LV afterload and wall tension, so **myocardial oxygen demand falls**. Haemodynamic assistance is modest and patient-dependent; IABP does not provide an independent fixed pump flow. It needs native LV ejection for effective support. Arrhythmia can impair timing but modern trigger modes can support AF/paced rhythms.

## Indications

- **Selected** severe LV failure/shock as a bridge to recovery/definitive treatment. Routine IABP for uncomplicated infarct-related cardiogenic shock is not recommended: IABP-SHOCK II did not reduce mortality. This current qualification updates the broad historical examiner list.
- **Failure to wean from bypass**, or low output after cardiac surgery.
- Post-infarction: refractory angina, ventricular arrhythmia, **mechanical complications** (acute mitral regurgitation, VSD) awaiting surgery.
- High-risk revascularisation (severe left main disease, poor LV function), or as a bridge to transplant or VAD; decompressing the LV during VA-ECMO.

## Contraindications

- **Aortic regurgitation** greater than mild (even mild AR can worsen, because diastolic augmentation increases regurgitant volume).
- **Aortic dissection** is a contraindication. Significant aneurysmal/other aortic disease or hostile graft anatomy requires expert anatomical assessment; avoid presenting every small aneurysm as an identical absolute contraindication.
- Severe aorto-iliac or peripheral vascular disease (limb ischaemia), and some graft or stent anatomy.
- Relative: coagulopathy (but frequent after bypass), local sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, bleeding, sepsis.

## Optimising performance

- **Position:** tip just distal to the left subclavian artery (about 2 cm below the aortic knob on chest X-ray).
- **Balloon volume:** appropriate size for the patient (full inflation).
- **Timing:** **inflation at the dicrotic notch** (start of diastole; too early closes the aortic valve prematurely and reduces stroke volume, too late loses augmentation), **deflation just before systole** at the end of diastole (late deflation raises afterload and opposes ejection); check the waveform on a 1:2 ratio and adjust.
- **Triggering:** ECG or arterial waveform; optimise rhythm/rate and device-specific AF or pacing trigger modes; tachycardia, ectopy or artefact can degrade timing.
- Maintain MAP and preload, correct arrhythmias, keep the leg straight, anticoagulate as appropriate, and check limb perfusion and haemolysis.
rubric: Explains diastolic augmentation and systolic unloading
Lists indications (shock, post-infarct, post-bypass, mechanical complications)
Lists contraindications (aortic regurgitation, aortic disease, vascular disease)
Notes coagulopathy as a relative contraindication
Position distal to the left subclavian artery and balloon volume
Describes inflation at diastole onset and deflation before systole in detail
Appropriate trigger/timing, including management of arrhythmia or pacing artefact

items.title: How does cardiac surgical arrest differ from routine ALS?
items.q: How does cardiac surgical arrest differ from routine ALS?
items.a:
- Use CALS-ANZ with a trained team; rapid rhythm confirmation and reversible-cause assessment.
- Witnessed monitored VF/pulseless VT may receive three stacked shocks; severe bradycardia/asystole may receive immediate epicardial pacing.
- Start CPR promptly if immediate treatment fails/is unavailable; arrange resternotomy within 5 minutes of arrest onset where indicated, including PEA/tamponade.
- This specialised pathway is for arrest after cardiac surgery, not a perfusing postoperative arrhythmia.

> **Closing point:** Prepare reopening and treat the arrest simultaneously.

items.title: 24. Complete heart block after aortic valve replacement
items.q: A patient develops symptomatic complete heart block after aortic valve replacement and has temporary epicardial pacing wires. Describe how you would set up and programme an external pacemaker, and how you would troubleshoot failure to capture.
items.a:
[BJA Education: Temporary epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery, 2023][TEMP]

### Types of temporary pacing

Transcutaneous, transvenous and epicardial pacing are the principal rescue options; transoesophageal pacing mainly stimulates the atrium and is not reliable ventricular rescue for complete AV block.

### Set-up for this patient

- **1.** **Assess ABCs and perfusion**, call the cardiac surgical/ICU team, attach ECG and a pulse-based monitor, and have external pacing/defibrillation ready. Symptomatic complete block needs effective **ventricular** pacing; AAI cannot bridge AV block.
- **2.** Check the generator battery, correct leads/cables, labelled atrial/ventricular wire pairs, connector security, insulation and manufacturer instructions. **Bipolar epicardial wires have both poles in the myocardium**. A unipolar system needs a dedicated return electrode—often subcutaneous—not an assumed ordinary surface ECG electrode. Do not improvise the connection or touch exposed conductors (microshock risk).
- **3.** Select **VVI** for ventricular rescue if only ventricular wires, AF or unreliable atrial sensing. **DDD** can preserve AV synchrony with reliable atrial/ventricular wires in sinus rhythm. AAI is only suitable when AV conduction is intact. Avoid unmonitored asynchronous pacing because of competitive R-on-T risk; reserve DOO/VOO for a specific indication with continuous observation.
- **4.** Set a rate suitable for perfusion (often 70–90/min initially after adult cardiac surgery, then titrate). In urgent failure, increase output sufficiently to achieve capture; once stable establish the capture threshold safely. Set **output generally at least twice the measured threshold**, within generator limits. Rate/output/sensing values are patient-specific, not guaranteed by a default setting.
- **5.** For dual-chamber pacing, set AV delay (often around 150–200 ms initially, then optimise clinically) and both atrial/ventricular output and sensitivity. Confirm **electrical and mechanical capture**, not simply pacing spikes.

### Threshold and sensing checks

- Perform checks only with trained staff, continuous monitoring and an immediately available rescue plan. **Do not deliberately lose capture in an unprotected pacing-dependent patient**. Test according to the local protocol, with backup pacing where required.
- Capture threshold is the lowest output producing consistent depolarisation; a rising threshold prompts review of wires, temperature, electrolytes and myocardium. A threshold >10 mA is concerning and requires an urgent reliable alternative rather than accepting a small safety margin.
- Sensing threshold is the smallest intrinsic signal reliably detected. If no intrinsic rhythm exists, it cannot be safely measured in the usual way. Sensitivity is expressed in **mV: lower number = more sensitive**. A common programmed margin is about half the measured sensing threshold, while avoiding oversensing; follow the generator-specific protocol.

### Failure to capture

Pacing spike without atrial depolarisation or QRS, with absent expected pulse: **support perfusion and increase output immediately**. Check power, connections, correct port/polarity and wires; consider displacement/fracture, high threshold from oedema/ischaemia, hypothermia, acidosis/electrolytes or drugs. Check echo for tamponade/major postoperative causes of deterioration. Use functioning alternative wires or external pacing while arranging urgent transvenous/other rescue. Atropine may fail in infranodal block; a titrated adrenaline/isoprenaline infusion can bridge to pacing where appropriate, without delaying it.

### Failure to sense

**Undersensing:** intrinsic beats are missed and inappropriate spikes may land on T waves; check leads and lower the mV setting to increase sensitivity. **Oversensing:** EMI/myopotentials are mistaken for beats, inhibiting pacing and causing pauses; remove interference, check wires and increase the mV setting if appropriate. Any R-on-T VT/VF requires immediate resuscitation/defibrillation and expert correction of the pacing system.

### Ongoing care

Document settings, capture/sensing thresholds, dependence and backup plan; inspect/check regularly (usually at least daily early after surgery). Persistent AV block requires cardiology assessment; timing of a permanent device depends on operation, escape rhythm, recovery and stability rather than a compulsory day-7 rule.

**Key evidence:** [TEMP][TEMP] · [BRADY][BRADY]

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises complete block requires reliable ventricular pacing and cannot be treated by AAI
- Checks labelled wires, battery, insulated connections and bipolar/unipolar return arrangements
- Selects VVI or DDD appropriately and confirms mechanical capture
- Sets rate, output, sensitivity and AV delay with a safe capture margin
- Avoids unprotected threshold testing in a pacing-dependent patient
- Troubleshoots failure to capture while providing immediate backup pacing
- Explains lower mV = greater sensitivity, oversensing pauses and undersensing R-on-T
- Documents daily checks, escalation and individualised permanent-pacing review

items.title: 25. Failing RV at separation from bypass (primary Set 13 overlap)
items.q: You cannot wean a patient from cardiopulmonary bypass after valve surgery because the right ventricle is failing. Describe your diagnosis and management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** Source-specific clinical checks and review depth are recorded in the audit register; examiner priorities are stated separately below.

### Look for the cause while you stabilise

Right ventricular (RV) failure after bypass can spiral: hypotension reduces right coronary perfusion, which worsens RV function and then LV filling. Causes are pre-existing RV dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension, long bypass or poor myocardial protection, protamine-associated pulmonary hypertension, LVAD insertion (RV failure in 20 to 40%) or heart transplantation (long ischaemic time, size mismatch), and **right coronary obstruction**: inadequate de-airing is among the commonest causes because the right coronary ostium is anterior and air collects there; also graft problems, ostial injury and thrombus.

### Diagnosis

On **TOE** check the RV free wall, septum (flattened or displaced towards the LV), RV:LV size ratio interpreted by view, loading and the full examination (not a universal diagnostic cutoff of 0.6), TAPSE below 1.7 cm (interpret cautiously after bypass and sternotomy), fractional area change below 35%, TR velocity interpreted with image quality and the absence/presence of RVOT obstruction; a value alone does not diagnose acute RV failure, and look for air and RCA flow. Haemodynamics: CVP above 20 mmHg or above wedge pressure, cardiac index below 2.1, and direct pressure/flow assessment for suspected RVOT obstruction; neither CVP nor a single pressure gradient establishes the whole diagnosis. The pulmonary artery pulsatility index has no agreed threshold.

### Management in order

- **1.** **Preload:** if low, a small challenge preferably with pump blood; if high, remove blood into the circuit, controlled volume removal/ultrafiltration; venodilation only when perfusion pressure and the cause permit it.
- **2.** **Ventilation:** FiO2 1.0, avoid hypercarbia, acidaemia, large tidal volume and high PEEP, with gentle recruitment.
- **3.** **Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators first line:** nitric oxide 10 to 20 ppm (up to 40), or inhaled milrinone, epoprostenol or iloprost; intravenous vasodilators only if these fail, because of systemic hypotension. Intratracheal milrinone has only limited observational support; it is not a standard rescue dose/route and must not substitute for a validated inhaled delivery protocol.
- **4.** **Perfusion pressure:** selected low-dose vasopressin may support SVR with relatively favourable PVR effects, but effects are dose-dependent and it is not universally ideal; cautious noradrenaline; phenylephrine raises PVR more.
- **5.** **Inotropy:** dobutamine first, then adrenaline or milrinone (milrinone causes more hypotension); adrenaline bolus and infusion for severe compromise.
- **6.** **Rhythm:** restore sinus rhythm, atrial epicardial pacing, pace heart block.
- **7.** **Escalate:** return promptly to adequate CPB support while correcting a mechanical/coronary cause if separation is unsafe, then selected VA-ECMO or RVAD. IABP may help selected associated LV/ischaemic problems; it does not directly support isolated RV output. Treat the cause: de-air, re-graft or revise a right coronary problem.

### Evidence

The chapter recommends routine haemodynamic monitoring, TOE and direct inspection for every case; most recommendations come from case series and expert opinion.

### Source safety check: vasopressin and perfusion support

The 2021 Blue Book RV chapter (p111) prints **1–4 units/min**. Do **not** use that value: it is incompatible with usual low-dose vasopressin practice. A current regional reference gives **0.6–2.4 units/hour**, equivalent to **0.01–0.04 units/min**, with titration under the local ICU protocol; monitor for ischaemic effects. A 2026 BJA Education corrigendum also identifies the same erroneous units/min range in the older RV review. This audit does not claim a formal Blue Book erratum. Noradrenaline is titrated to perfusion and haemodynamics; an old review's 0.2 microgram/kg/min suggestion is not a universal maximum. Vasopressin's PVR effects are dose-dependent, not guaranteed zero.

### Practical integration

Distinguish primary RV contractile failure from excessive PVR, inadequate preload, a new valve lesion, dynamic RVOT obstruction, tamponade and LV distension. Notify the surgeon and perfusionist early and reassess after each intervention; repeated attempts to separate from bypass with severe hypotension compound myocardial injury. Maintain appropriate coronary and systemic perfusion and verify de-airing and the surgical repair. Use serial TOE, arterial pressure, mixed venous oxygenation and lactate trends to assess whether the circulation actually improves rather than treating a single pressure number. Postoperative handover must specify RV loading conditions, inotrope/vasopressor targets, pacing mode and reliable capture, pulmonary vasodilator delivery/weaning, fluid strategy and the threshold for mechanical support.

## Self-marking checklist
- Causes (air in right coronary, protamine, pre-existing PH, LVAD, poor protection)
- Diagnosis on TOE and haemodynamics
- Preload and ventilation strategy
- Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators
- Vasopressor and inotrope choices
- Rhythm and pacing
- Mechanical support and return to bypass
- Evidence summary

items.title: 26. Polymorphic VT with epicardial wires in DDD
items.q: A patient with temporary epicardial wires develops recurrent polymorphic VT despite a normal QT. The pacing box is in DDD mode and pacing spikes appear near T waves. Explain the mechanism and your management.
items.a:
### Recognise a pacing-induced arrhythmia

Assess pulse and circulation immediately. Sustained unstable polymorphic VT or VF requires **unsynchronised defibrillation** and the applicable resuscitation pathway; do not wait for synchronisation or a full device analysis. Ask for cardiac surgery/ICU and EP assistance and review saved telemetry without delaying rescue. Stop the pacing system from continuing to trigger unsafe impulses while providing resuscitation and a reliable alternative if the patient is dependent. Simply turning off all pacing and leaving a dependent patient unsupported is unsafe.

### Why a demand mode can still produce R-on-T

Demand pacing is safe only when intrinsic signals are sensed reliably. **Undersensing** may result from poor wire signal, migration, cable/connection problems or a sensitivity value set too high. Inappropriate impulses can then fall during ventricular repolarisation and trigger polymorphic VT/VF. Normal QT does not exclude this mechanism and does not make the rhythm torsades de pointes.

In DDD pacing, poor **atrial** sensing can also provoke ventricular R-on-T. An unsensed intrinsic P wave may be followed by an inappropriate atrial impulse overlapping a conducted ventricular beat. Ventricular blanking after that atrial impulse can conceal the true R wave; the box subsequently emits a ventricular impulse after its programmed AV interval, potentially onto the T wave. Thus the atrial circuit and timing need review, not only the ventricular output. Higher output does not repair an inability to sense intrinsic activity.

### Restore a safe system

Review dependence, underlying atrial/ventricular rhythm and perfusion. Check the patient, wires, connections and generator systematically; correct hypothermia, hypoxia, K/Mg/Ca abnormalities, acidosis and ischaemia. Confirm settings and inspect for oversensing, crosstalk, tracking of AF/flutter or pacemaker-mediated re-entry. These mechanisms need different solutions.

With expert staff and immediate rescue available, establish sensing and capture thresholds when safe. **Lower mV setting means greater sensitivity**; set an appropriate margin below the measured intrinsic signal without producing noise oversensing. If no intrinsic rhythm exists, routine sensing measurement is not possible. If the patient does not need pacing, leaving an unreliable backup system switched on can add danger: an expert may turn it off and continue observation. If dependent, use a reliably functioning simpler mode/wire system or urgent transvenous/new epicardial support, maintaining intensive monitoring. Asynchronous mode is a supervised emergency option when necessary, not routine ward backup.

### Prevent recurrence and identify complications

Verify electrical and mechanical capture and monitor continuously after any change. A low rate setting is not inherently safe in an inadequately sensing DDD system. Document thresholds, settings, dependence, rationale and backup plan, checking at least daily and after major clinical changes. Do not transfer a patient with unreliable sensing to an unmonitored ward.

The same safety review includes wire removal: coordinate pacing need, coagulation/antithrombotics and local removal policy. Resistance requires stopping and surgical advice. New shock after removal needs urgent echo for tamponade; the observation plan must continue after the wire is out. Evidence is largely practical/observational, but the mechanisms and preventable hazards are directly relevant to external pacemaker programming outcomes. [TEMP][TEMP]

## Self-marking checklist
- Treats sustained polymorphic VT/VF immediately
- Identifies R-on-T from undersensing rather than assuming long-QT torsades
- Explains the atrial-sensing/ventricular-blanking DDD mechanism
- Protects pacing-dependent patients during system interruption
- Distinguishes output from sensing and lower mV from greater numerical sensitivity
- Uses a systematic patient–wire–generator check and a reliable alternative
- Avoids unsafe ward backup and documents daily checks
- Recognises wire-removal tamponade and plans surveillance

items.title: 2026.1 Q7: Epicardial pacing in complete heart block before separation from bypass
items.q: A patient is in complete heart block prior to separation from cardiopulmonary bypass. Outline the programming considerations for epicardial pacing in this patient. (30%) Describe your approach to troubleshooting intermittent capture of the pacemaker in this patient who is pacing-dependent in the ICU. (70%)
items.model:
> **Examiner-report focus:** Select and justify a reasonable rate and mode. The 70% troubleshooting component needs a systematic patient–leads–generator approach and alternative modalities that keep a pacing-dependent patient safe. Directly allocated to BT_RT 1.37 and SS_CS 1.11, despite the CPB setting.

### Programming before separation (30%)

Confirm complete block, underlying atrial rhythm, functioning atrial/ventricular wires and the patient's haemodynamics with the surgeon and perfusionist. Reliable **ventricular capture** is essential: AAI cannot treat complete AV block. Select **DDD/AV-sequential pacing** if atrial activity, sensing and both sets of wires are reliable; use **VVI** for AF, inadequate atrial wires or a simpler dependable rescue. Choose a rate such as **80–90/min initially**, then titrate to arterial pressure, output, filling and ischaemia rather than quoting a rate without justification. Too slow reduces output; excessive rate reduces filling and increases myocardial oxygen demand. Optimise AV delay if sequential pacing is used, commonly starting around 150–200 ms, guided by haemodynamics.

Check battery, generator, labelled connections and polarity according to the actual bipolar or unipolar system; a skin return electrode is not used with every bipolar pair. Establish capture threshold safely and set a margin, commonly **2–3 times threshold**, within the generator's limits. A high/unstable threshold before closure needs attention to wires/position rather than acceptance of unreliable capture. Set demand sensing appropriately; **lower mV means greater sensitivity**. Asynchronous pacing may be necessary with interference in the open theatre, but is not routine unattended ICU backup. Confirm a paced QRS **and mechanical pulse/arterial waveform**.

### Immediate ICU safety (70%)

Call for experienced cardiac/ICU help, assess pulse, BP, perfusion, oxygenation and the rhythm. For haemodynamic compromise from failure to capture, increase ventricular output immediately while preparing **transcutaneous pacing**, a spare functioning generator/cable and urgent transvenous or surgical wire rescue. Provide chronotropic/vasopressor support as a bridge when appropriate. Pulselessness requires the applicable cardiac-surgical resuscitation pathway. Do not repeatedly lower output or disconnect wires to demonstrate dependence in an unprotected patient.

### Systematic diagnosis and correction

- **1.** **Patient:** determine whether spikes occur without QRS (noncapture), absent spikes (failure to pace/oversensing), or QRS without useful output (mechanical/circulatory problem). Correct hypothermia, hypoxia, acidosis, K/Mg/Ca disturbance, ischaemia and drug effects. Assess bleeding, tamponade, severe ventricular dysfunction and mechanical surgical problems with urgent echo when indicated.
- **2.** **Leads and connections:** follow the circuit from patient to box. Check migration at the skin, labelling, loose connectors, exposed conductors, fracture, wrong ports/polarity and damaged reusable cables. Replace a suspect cable; use functioning alternative wires if available.
- **3.** **Generator/settings:** verify power/battery, mode, rate, output and chamber assignment; review sensing, refractory/blanking settings and interference. Respiratory variation in threshold near the programmed output can cause intermittent noncapture. Replace the generator when necessary. Increasing output will not correct inhibition caused by oversensing; treat that mechanism separately.
- **4.** **Sensing complications:** oversensing inhibits output—remove EMI/shivering and consider a higher mV value. Undersensing allows inappropriate impulses/R-on-T—check the system and lower the mV value if appropriate. Complex DDD timing can be dangerous with poor atrial sensing; simplify the mode under expert supervision.

Reassess electrical and mechanical capture after every change. Continue continuous monitoring, record settings/thresholds/dependence and ensure a named backup plan. Repeat checks at least daily and after significant changes; do not transfer a dependent patient with unreliable wires to an inadequately monitored area. Permanent-device timing depends on the operation, recovery and escape rhythm, not a universal day number. [TEMP][TEMP]
rubric: Justifies ventricular-capable mode and rate for complete block
Explains output/capture margin, sensing and AV synchrony
Confirms mechanical as well as electrical capture
Protects perfusion immediately and supplies backup pacing
Uses patient–lead–generator troubleshooting
Distinguishes noncapture, oversensing and undersensing
Corrects reversible physiology and considers tamponade/ischaemia
Documents monitoring, reassessment and escalation

items.title: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.q: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.a:
- Cardiac denervation makes the atropine/glycopyrrolate chronotropic response unreliable; variable reinnervation prevents an absolute rule.
- Resting rate is often around 90–100; reflex compensation may be blunted.
- For important bradycardia prepare direct chronotropy (e.g. isoprenaline/adrenaline as appropriate) and pacing.
- Ephedrine has mixed direct/indirect action, with variable response.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.q: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.a:
- Ephedrine: mixed direct/indirect effects; less predictable after denervation.
- Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine: exaggerated.
- Phenylephrine and metaraminol: effective, no reflex bradycardia.
- Adenosine: exaggerated bradycardia.
- Neostigmine: bradycardia possible.

> **Closing point:** Titrate catecholamines carefully.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.q: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.a:
- No reflex tachycardia; preload dependent.
- Silent ischaemia: no angina.
- Arrhythmia and pacing requirements vary with surgical technique, timing and cohort; investigate new arrhythmia for rejection or vasculopathy.
- Re-innervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months).
- Ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or vasculopathy.

> **Closing point:** No reflex means volume matters most.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: 27. Heart transplant recipient for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient who received a heart transplant 3 years ago presents for non-cardiac surgery. Describe the physiology of the transplanted heart and the implications for anaesthetic drugs and management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2019, "Perioperative management of heart transplantation" (Edwards, Allen).

### Physiology of the denervated heart

- Vagal and sympathetic supply is cut. The SA node runs at its intrinsic rate of **90 to 100 beats/min**.
- The heart cannot mount a reflex tachycardia to hypovolaemia, vasodilation or afterload change; cardiac output depends on **preload** and slow rise of circulating catecholamines. It is "preload dependent".
- Angina may be absent, so **ischaemia can be silent**, although reinnervation may restore symptoms. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is suspected from new wall motion or diastolic abnormalities or ventricular arrhythmias; coronary angiography with IVUS/OCT and other modalities is selected by the transplant service; IVUS can detect early intimal disease but is not the sole diagnostic test.
- Reinnervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months, parasympathetic 1 to 3 years).
- Arrhythmias: conduction delay and heart block, arrhythmia and pacing rates vary by timing, surgical technique and cohort; ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or CAV. Double P waves can occur. Carotid sinus massage and Valsalva have no effect.

### Drug responses

| Drug | Effect |
|---|---|
| Atropine, glycopyrrolate | Usually absent/unreliable response; variable reinnervation; use direct chronotropy/pacing |
| Ephedrine | Mixed direct/indirect; effect can be reduced or unpredictable |
| Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine | Exaggerated (more adrenoreceptors): titrate |
| Phenylephrine, metaraminol | Effective, no reflex bradycardia |
| Isoprenaline | Effective; use for bradycardia |
| Adenosine | Exaggerated bradycardia |
| Neostigmine | Bradycardia possible, especially beyond 6 months |

### Other issues

BJA Education 2021 (heart transplantation) adds that **primary graft dysfunction** is the main cause of early death, and that mechanical support (ideally ECMO) should be started early when graft dysfunction does not respond to moderate-dose inotropes.


Immunosuppression (calcineurin inhibitors: nephrotoxicity; continue on time), infection risk (asepsis, antibiotics), malignancy (more than 10% develop de novo cancer; skin cancers 100 times), tricuspid regurgitation, and drug interactions with tacrolimus or ciclosporin. Monitor ECG, arterial line for major surgery, and warm, preload-aware induction.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains denervation, resting rate of 90 to 100 and absent reflex tachycardia
- Notes preload dependence and silent ischaemia
- Describes atropine/glycopyrrolate responses as unreliable and names direct chronotropy/pacing alternatives
- Describes exaggerated responses to catecholamines
- Mentions CAV, arrhythmias and pacemaker risk
- Covers immunosuppression and infection precautions

**Audit evidence map:** BB19; ISHLT23. Source depth and any limitations are recorded in the audit register.
